questions.stemHtml: Identify the nerve root(s) of the thickened nerve marked by the arrow in the image shown below?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) C2, C3

 

The thickened nerve marked in the image is the great auricular nerve, which provides sensory innervation to the skin over the angle of the mandible and the ear (pinna). The great auricular nerve arises from the cervical plexus, formed by the ventral rami of the C2 and C3 spinal nerves. It runs upwards across the sternocleidomastoid muscle and is one of the four cutaneous branches of the cervical plexus.

 

 

This nerve has two divisions:

 

Anterior division: Supplies the skin over the angle of the mandible.

 

Posterior division: Supplies the skin over the pinna of the ear.

 

The region innervated by the great auricular nerve is commonly referred to as the "shaving area", and this nerve is involved in conditions like Frey’s syndrome.

 

Other Options:

 

Option. A, C1: The C1 spinal nerve does not contribute to the formation of the great auricular nerve. Instead, it primarily contributes to the ansa cervicalis, which innervates some of the strap muscles of the neck.

 

Educational objective:

 

The great auricular nerve arises from the C2 and C3 spinal nerve roots and provides sensory innervation to the skin over the angle of the mandible and the ear (pinna).

questions.stem: Wernicke’s area is situated in the:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Superior temporal gyrus

 

 

Wernicke’s area is responsible for the comprehension of speech and language. It is located in Brodmann area 22, which lies in the superior temporal gyrus of the brain's dominant hemisphere (usually the left hemisphere). This area is part of the temporal lobe and is closely associated with the processing and understanding of spoken and written language. Damage to Wernicke's area results in Wernicke's aphasia, a condition where a person may speak fluently, but their speech often lacks meaning, and they have difficulty understanding language.

 

The superior temporal gyrus is located below the lateral sulcus (also known as the Sylvian fissure) and is involved in both auditory processing and language comprehension, which aligns with the function of Wernicke’s area.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Inferior frontal gyrus: This is incorrect because the inferior frontal gyrus contains Broca's area (Brodmann areas 44 and 45), which is responsible for speech production, not comprehension. It is located in the frontal lobe.

 

Option C. Angular gyrus: While the angular gyrus is involved in language, particularly reading and writing, it is not where Wernicke’s area is located. The angular gyrus is located in the parietal lobe.

 

Option D. Postcentral gyrus: This is incorrect as the postcentral gyrus is the primary sensory area (Brodmann area 3, 1, 2), located in the parietal lobe, and has no direct involvement in speech comprehension.

 

Educational objectives:

 

Wernicke’s area is located in the superior temporal gyrus (Brodmann area 22) and is responsible for the comprehension of speech and language.

questions.stem: Which of these is not a type of synovial joint?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Symphysis pubis

 

 

The symphysis pubis is a type of secondary cartilaginous joint, not a synovial joint. In secondary cartilaginous joints, bones are connected by a fibrocartilaginous pad or disk, and there is little to no movement. The symphysis pubis is a good example of this type of joint, as it consists of fibrocartilage between the two pubic bones, allowing slight movement for pelvic flexibility during childbirth and general movement.

 

On the other hand, synovial joints are characterized by the presence of a joint cavity filled with synovial fluid, which allows free movement of the bones. They are the most common type of joint in the body and allow for various types of movement depending on the joint subtype (e.g., hinge, ball-and-socket, pivot).

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Costotransverse joint: This is a type of plane synovial joint, found between the transverse processes of the vertebrae and the ribs. It allows slight gliding movements, which assist in breathing.

 

Option B. Costovertebral joint: This joint is also a plane synovial joint located between the ribs and the vertebral bodies. It permits slight movements to accommodate lung expansion during respiration.

 

Option C. Radiocarpal joint: This is an ellipsoid synovial joint (also known as a condyloid joint), located between the radius and the carpal bones of the wrist, allowing flexion, extension, abduction, and adduction of the wrist.

 

Educational objectives:

 

The symphysis pubis is a secondary cartilaginous joint, not a synovial joint

questions.stem: Which among the following is incorrect regarding Sibson's fascia?

options.label: A
options.text: Attached to the inner border of 2nd rib

questions.answerText: Attached to the inner border of 2nd rib
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Attached to the inner border of 2nd rib

 

 

 

 

Sibson’s fascia, also known as the suprapleural membrane, is attached to the inner border of the first rib, not the second rib. It extends from the transverse process of the C7 vertebra to the inner border of the first rib, not the second rib.

 

Sibson’s fascia covers the apical part of the lung. This membrane separates the lung from structures in the neck and provides additional support at the thoracic inlet. Above the lung, it forms a protective layer known as the cervical pleura.

 

The fascia is associated with the scalenus minimus muscle. Anatomically, it is considered a remnant of the scalenus minimus, which is a small muscle located in the neck.

 

Furthermore, the subclavian artery and subclavian vein pass above Sibson’s fascia. These vessels traverse this area as they course through the thoracic inlet, making it a significant structure in relation to important vasculature.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Covers apical part of lung: This is correct. Sibson’s fascia indeed covers the apical part of the lung, helping to separate and protect the uppermost portion of the lung from the neck region.

 

Option C. Part of scalenus minimus muscle: This is correct. Sibson’s fascia is considered to be a remnant of the scalenus minimus muscle, a small muscle in the neck.

 

Option D. Vessels pass above the fascia: This is correct. The subclavian artery and subclavian vein pass above Sibson’s fascia as they enter or leave the thoracic cavity.

 

Educational objectives:

 

Sibson's fascia is attached to the inner border of the first rib (not the second rib) and extends between the transverse process of the C7 vertebra and the first rib. It covers the apical part of the lung and is a remnant of the scalenus minimus muscle. The subclavian artery and vein pass above this fascia.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man presents with sudden severe chest pain. He has a history of hypertension, and you suspect aortic dissection. An urgent CT scan shows a widened aorta with a false lumen but no obvious signs of rupture. You note to your consultant that the dissection extends to the level of the aortic opening of the diaphragm, and express your concern about possible damage to all the structures that pass through the aortic opening of the diaphragm. These structures include all of the following except :
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Vagal trunk

 

 

The aortic opening, or aortic hiatus, is located at the T12 level of the diaphragm. Structures that pass through this opening include the aorta, the thoracic duct, and the azygous vein. These are clearly identified in the image and mentioned during the discussion.

 

The vagal trunk, however, does not pass through the aortic opening. It passes through the esophageal hiatus located at the T10 level. The esophageal hiatus transmits the esophagus, anterior and posterior vagal trunks, and the esophageal branches of the left gastric artery and vein.

 

Therefore, the vagal trunk is the correct answer, as it does not pass through the aortic opening but instead through the esophageal hiatus.

 

Other Options:

Option B. Azygous vein: This is correct. The azygous vein also passes through the aortic opening, 

 

Option C. Thoracic duct: This is correct. The thoracic duct, which drains lymph from most of the body, passes through the aortic opening of the diaphragm.

questions.stemHtml: What is the function of the muscle marked in the image below, at the metacarpophalangeal joint?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Flexion

 

The muscles marked in the image are the lumbricals. These muscles originate from the tendons of the flexor digitorum profundus and insert into the dorsal digital expansion of the fingers. Their main function at the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joint is to produce flexion. At the same time, they produce extension at the interphalangeal (IP) joints.

 

This unique dual action—flexion at the MCP joints and extension at the IP joints—allows for the precision movements needed for tasks like holding a pen or delicate object, known as the pen-holding position. If the lumbricals are damaged, this can result in a claw hand deformity, which occurs when the MCP joints are extended and the IP joints are flexed.

 

In conditions such as ulnar nerve damage (affecting lumbricals L3 and L4) or median nerve damage (affecting lumbricals L1 and L2), this function is impaired, leading to difficulties with finger movements.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Extension: Incorrect. The lumbricals cause extension at the interphalangeal joints, not at the metacarpophalangeal joints.

 

Option C. Abduction: Incorrect. Abduction (movement away from the midline of the hand) is not a function of the lumbricals. This action is performed by the dorsal interossei muscles.

 

Option D. Adduction: Incorrect. Adduction (movement towards the midline of the hand) is also not a function of the lumbricals. This is performed by the palmar interossei muscles.

 

Educational objectives:

 

The lumbricals produce flexion at the metacarpophalangeal joints and extension at the interphalangeal joints. Damage to these muscles or their nerve supply can lead to deformities like claw hand.

questions.stem: Following surgery for varicose veins, the patient is experiencing a complaint of sensory loss in the medial area of the leg and foot. Which of the following nerves is the most probable site of injury?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Saphenous nerve

 

In varicose vein surgery, especially involving the great saphenous vein, the saphenous nerve is at risk of injury. This nerve provides sensation to the medial side of the leg and foot, which aligns with the patient’s complaint of sensory loss in the medial region.

 

During the surgery, the saphenous nerve, running along the great saphenous vein, can easily be damaged due to its close proximity to the vein. As a result, patients may experience sensory loss in the medial leg and foot, exactly as reported in this case.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Sural nerve: The sural nerve supplies sensation to the lateral side of the leg and foot. An injury to this nerve would not result in sensory loss on the medial side.

 

Option B. Superficial peroneal nerve: This nerve innervates the dorsum of the foot, not the medial leg or foot, which makes it unrelated to the symptoms described.

 

Option C. Deep peroneal nerve: The deep peroneal nerve supplies sensation to a small area between the first and second toes. It does not affect the medial side of the leg or foot.

 

Educational objectives:

 

During surgery for varicose veins, the saphenous nerve is susceptible to injury, leading to sensory loss in the medial leg and foot, as it runs along the great saphenous vein.

questions.stemHtml: Identify the cartilage shown below:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) White fibrocartilage

 

The cartilage shown is white fibrocartilage. It can be identified by the presence of "thick, red, wavy bundles" that are a distinct feature of fibrocartilage. This type of cartilage is structured with densely layered collagen fibers, which provide strength and durability. Fibrocartilage is typically found in areas of the body that experience high pressure and tension, such as intervertebral discs and the pubic symphysis.

 

 

The thick, wavy collagen bundles confirm that this is fibrocartilage.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Non-articular hyaline cartilage: This type of cartilage would have a homogeneous blue appearance due to the presence of hyaluronic acid. Since the image shows red, wavy bundles instead, this option is incorrect.

 

 

Option B. Articular hyaline cartilage: Similar to non-articular hyaline cartilage, articular hyaline cartilage also appears smooth and blue. The absence of this feature rules it out.

 

 

Option C. Yellow cartilage: Yellow cartilage, also called elastic cartilage, contains visible elastic fibers arranged in a "single, double" pattern. The lack of these fibers in the image rules out this option.

questions.stem: During a yawn, a student experienced a jaw-locking incident. Identify the muscle attached to the articular disc of the temporomandibular joint:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Lateral pterygoid

 

The lateral pterygoid muscle plays a key role in the movement of the temporomandibular joint (TMJ). It is the only muscle of mastication that is directly attached to the articular disc of the TMJ. This muscle helps with the protraction (forward movement) of the mandible. During movements like yawning, the lateral pterygoid contracts, pulling the mandible forward, and this action can occasionally result in jaw-locking if the mandible becomes stuck in front of the zygomatic tubercle, as described in the provided material. This forward movement is essential for various functions like opening the mouth wide and moving the jaw side-to-side.

 

The articular disc moves forward and downward during this action, allowing the jaw to open. If the movement goes too far or happens suddenly (like during a yawn), it can result in the jaw getting stuck in a protracted position, causing the jaw-locking condition.

 

 

Other Options:

Option B Temporalis: The temporalis is responsible for elevating the mandible (closing the mouth) and retruding the jaw. It is not attached to the articular disc of the temporomandibular joint and is therefore incorrect in this context.

 

Option C. Medial pterygoid: The medial pterygoid assists with elevating the mandible and moving it side to side. It has no direct attachment to the articular disc and doesn't contribute to protraction of the jaw.

 

Option D. Masseter: The masseter is primarily involved in elevating the mandible for jaw closure. Like the other incorrect options, it is not attached to the articular disc.

 

Educational objectives:

 

The lateral pterygoid is the only muscle attached to the articular disc of the temporomandibular joint and is responsible for protracting the mandible. Prolonged or excessive contraction during actions like yawning can lead to jaw locking.

questions.stemHtml: A patient was undergoing clinical evaluation during which the marked structure was stimulated. Which of the following nerves was being tested?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) IX

 

The marked structure in the image represents the palatine area, most likely involving the soft palate or tonsillar region. When this area is stimulated, the nerve being tested is the glossopharyngeal nerve (Cranial Nerve IX). The glossopharyngeal nerve carries the sensory input from this region, including the palatal and pharyngeal mucosa, which is involved in the palatal (gag) reflex.

 

During the palatal reflex (also known as the gag reflex), sensory information from the soft palate is relayed to the brainstem (medulla oblongata) via Cranial Nerve IX. The motor response is then carried out by Cranial Nerve X (the vagus nerve), which stimulates the muscles of the pharynx and palate.

 

Although Cranial Nerve X also plays a role in the motor aspect of this reflex, the primary sensory nerve being tested is Cranial Nerve IX, 

 

Other Options:

Option D. Cranial Nerve XII: The hypoglossal nerve controls the movements of the tongue and is unrelated to the sensory or motor components of the gag reflex.

 

Educational objectives:

questions.stemHtml: Which nerve innervates the marked muscle?

options.label: C
options.text: From the dorsal rami of C1

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Dorsal scapular nerve

 

 

 

The muscle marked in the image is the levator scapulae, responsible for elevating the scapula. This muscle, along with the rhomboid major and rhomboid minor, is innervated by the dorsal scapular nerve. The dorsal scapular nerve arises from the root of C5 and provides motor innervation to these muscles. The levator scapulae helps lift the scapula upwards, an action that is crucial for shoulder movement and stability.

 

The dorsal scapular nerve, originating from the brachial plexus, specifically innervates the levator scapulae, rhomboid major, and rhomboid minor muscles, allowing for the elevation and retraction of the scapula.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Suprascapular nerve: The suprascapular nerve innervates the supraspinatus and infraspinatus muscles, both of which are involved in shoulder rotation and abduction, but it does not innervate the levator scapulae.

 

Option C. From the dorsal rami of C1: The dorsal rami of C1 primarily innervates the suboccipital muscles at the base of the skull and do not provide innervation to the levator scapulae or rhomboids.

 

Option D. Subscapular nerve: The subscapular nerve innervates the subscapularis and teres major muscles, which are responsible for internal rotation and adduction of the humerus. It is not involved with the levator scapulae.

 

Educational objectives:

 

The dorsal scapular nerve (C5) innervates the levator scapulae, rhomboid major, and rhomboid minor muscles, playing a crucial role in the elevation and retraction of the scapula.

questions.stem: All the following are true about the right coronary artery except:

options.label: A
options.text: Its diameter is less than left coronary artery

options.label: B
options.text: It arises from the anterior aortic sinus

options.label: C
options.text: It gives rise to circumflex coronary branch

options.label: D
options.text: Right conus artery is its first branch

questions.answerText: It gives rise to circumflex coronary branch
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) It gives rise to circumflex coronary branch

 

The right coronary artery (RCA) is responsible for supplying blood to parts of the right atrium, right ventricle, and portions of the conduction system. Several statements about the RCA are true, but the incorrect statement here is that it "gives rise to the circumflex coronary branch," which is false because the circumflex branch arises from the left coronary artery (LCA), not the right.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Its diameter is less than left coronary artery: This is correct. The RCA generally has a smaller diameter compared to the LCA, which supplies a larger area of the heart.

 

Option B. It arises from the anterior aortic sinus: This is correct. The RCA originates from the anterior (right) aortic sinus of the ascending aorta.

 

Option D. Right conus artery is its first branch: This is correct. The right conus artery is typically the first branch of the RCA and supplies the conus arteriosus.

 

Educational objectives:

 

The circumflex coronary artery arises from the left coronary artery, not the right. The right coronary artery is responsible for supplying specific parts of the heart and has a smaller diameter than the left coronary artery.

questions.stem: All of the following structures are derived from the aponeurosis of the external oblique muscle except:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Linea semilunaris

 

The external oblique aponeurosis contributes to several important anatomical structures. Among these, the pectineal ligament, inguinal ligament, and lacunar ligament are direct derivatives of the external oblique aponeurosis. These structures are essential in the formation of the lower abdominal wall and the pelvic region.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Pectineal ligament: Formed from the external oblique aponeurosis as it attaches along the pectineal line of the pubis.

 

Option B. Inguinal ligament: This is a well-known derivative of the external oblique aponeurosis, running from the anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) to the pubic tubercle.

 

Option C. Lacunar ligament: This triangular ligament forms from the fibers of the external oblique aponeurosis as it extends near the medial part of the inguinal ligament.

 

However, the linea semilunaris is not derived from the external oblique aponeurosis. It is a curved tendinous line that marks the lateral border of the rectus abdominis muscle and does not originate from external oblique aponeurosis.

 

 

Educational objectives:

 

The linea semilunaris is not a derivative of the external oblique aponeurosis, unlike the pectineal, inguinal, and lacunar ligaments.

Option B. Basket cells: Basket cells are interneurons found in the molecular layer of the cerebellum. They do not have the distinct large, flask-shaped appearance that is characteristic of Purkinje cells.

 

Option C. Golgi cells: Golgi cells are inhibitory interneurons located in the granular layer of the cerebellum. They are much smaller than Purkinje cells and have a different morphology.

The cerebellar cortex is organized into three layers:

 

Molecular layer (outermost): Contains the dendrites of Purkinje cells, molecular cells, and basket cells.

 

Purkinje cell layer (middle): Contains the large flask-shaped Purkinje cell bodies.

 

Granular layer (innermost): Contains densely packed granule cells.

 

The Purkinje cells are crucial for the integration of sensory and motor inputs and coordination of movement. They serve as the primary inhibitory output of the cerebellar cortex.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a projection from a bone surface?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Trabeculae

 

 

Trabeculae are not projections from a bone surface but rather internal structures found within spongy (cancellous) bone. Trabeculae form a mesh-like network that supports the bone from the inside, providing strength while keeping the bone lightweight. They are seen in areas such as the ends of long bones, vertebrae, and the interior of flat bones.

 

Other options:


Option A. Trochanter: A large, blunt projection found on the femur (e.g., greater and lesser trochanters), used for muscle attachment.
 

Option B. Tubercle: A small, rounded projection, usually where tendons or ligaments attach, found on bones like the humerus (greater and lesser tubercles).
 

Option D. Tuberosity: A large, rough projection where muscles and tendons attach, such as the ischial tuberosity on the pelvis or the deltoid tuberosity on the humerus.

 

Educational Objective:


Trabeculae are internal bone structures that do not project from the surface, unlike trochanters, tubercles, and tuberosities, which are surface projections used for muscle and ligament attachment.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old male patient was admitted with complaints of acute pain in the right shoulder of three-days duration associated with swelling and he also had difficulty in using his right shoulder since then. Pain was sudden at onset, continuous, and moderate to severe in intensity and it was aggravated on activity. In addition, he had severe night and rest pain. He also gave a history of intramuscular injection of Iron in the right deltoid region 2 weeks previously, which was administered in a local clinic. On examination, there was a globular swelling in the lateral aspect of the right arm extending up to the scapular region. There was a local rise of temperature and tenderness over the swelling, painful restriction of the right shoulder movements and he could not abduct his arm to the right angle. MRI scan of the right shoulder showed pyomyositis of the posterior belly of the right deltoid muscle with central abscess formation. Which among the following is not a possible complication that can be expected in this case if untreated? Loss of sensation on lower lateral aspect of arm

options.label: A
options.text: Loss of sensation on lower lateral aspect of arm

options.label: C
options.text: Weak of flexion of arm at shoulder joint

options.label: D
options.text: Inability to extend the arm at shoulder joint

questions.answerText: Loss of sensation on lower lateral aspect of arm
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Loss of sensation on lower lateral aspect of arm

 

The deltoid muscle is primarily responsible for abduction of the shoulder. It is innervated by the axillary nerve, which also supplies sensation to the upper lateral aspect of the arm via its branch, the upper lateral cutaneous nerve. If the deltoid is involved in an abscess or infection, it can lead to complications such as weakness in shoulder movements (abduction, flexion, and extension), but loss of sensation on the lower lateral aspect of the arm is not expected because the axillary nerve affects the upper lateral part of the arm.

 

However, loss of sensation on the lower lateral aspect of the arm is not expected because the axillary nerve provides sensation to the upper lateral portion, not the lower lateral part of the arm.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Inability to abduct the shoulder: The deltoid is responsible for abduction, so this is a possible complication.

 

Option C. Weak flexion of arm at shoulder joint: The anterior fibers of the deltoid are involved in shoulder flexion, making this a potential complication.

 

Option D. Inability to extend the arm at shoulder joint: The posterior fibers of the deltoid assist in arm extension, so this is also a possible complication.

 

Educational objectives:

 

The axillary nerve provides sensation to the upper lateral aspect of the arm, and involvement of the deltoid muscle affects abduction, flexion, and extension of the arm. However, loss of sensation in the lower lateral aspect of the arm is not a likely complication.

options.label: A
options.text: Loss of taste sensation from anterior 2/3 tongue

options.label: B
options.text: Loss of taste sensation from posterior 1/3 tongue

options.label: C
options.text: Loss of general sensation from anterior 2/3 tongue

options.label: D
options.text: Loss of taste sensation from posterior most part of tongue

questions.answerText: Loss of taste sensation from anterior 2/3 tongue
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Loss of taste sensation from anterior 2/3 tongue

 

The nerve that lies medially to the spine of sphenoid is the chorda tympani, which is a branch of the facial nerve (Cranial Nerve VII). The chorda tympani nerve is responsible for carrying taste sensations from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue. If this nerve is injured, it would result in the loss of taste sensation from this part of the tongue.

 

The chorda tympani join the lingual nerve (a branch of the mandibular nerve, V3) and provides taste innervation to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue.

 

The spine of sphenoid serves as a landmark, and the chorda tympani runs medial to it, whereas the auriculotemporal nerve runs lateral to it.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Loss of taste sensation from posterior 1/3 tongue: This is incorrect because the posterior third of the tongue is innervated by the glossopharyngeal nerve (Cranial Nerve IX).

 

Option C. Loss of general sensation from anterior 2/3 tongue: The lingual nerve, a branch of the mandibular nerve, provides general sensation to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, not taste.

 

Option D. Loss of taste sensation from posterior most part of tongue: The vagus nerve (Cranial Nerve X) supplies taste to the posterior-most part of the tongue (near the epiglottis), not the chorda tympani.

 

Educational objectives:

 

Injury to the chorda tympani (a branch of the facial nerve) results in the loss of taste sensation from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, while general sensation is provided by the lingual nerve.

questions.stemHtml: A patient presents with a unilateral throbbing headache, photophobia, and excessive lacrimation. He also complains of hemifacial pain on clenching of teeth. On examination, pupillary reflex, light reflex, and accommodation reflex are normal. Which of the following marked nerves is involved in the above scenario?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) 3

 

The patient is presenting with symptoms typical of trigeminal neuralgia. This condition involves the trigeminal nerve (Cranial Nerve V), which is responsible for sensory innervation to the face, including pain and touch. The third marked structure in the image corresponds to the trigeminal nerve, which has three main branches: the ophthalmic (V1), maxillary (V2), and mandibular (V3) divisions.

 

The symptoms of unilateral throbbing headache, photophobia, lacrimation, and hemifacial pain on clenching of teeth all point towards trigeminal involvement. The normal pupillary, light, and accommodation reflexes indicate that the third cranial nerve (oculomotor nerve) is functioning normally, thus excluding it as the affected nerve in this case.

 

The ophthalmic division (V1) of the trigeminal nerve is responsible for sensory input from the upper face and could explain the photophobia and lacrimation.

 

The maxillary division (V2) and mandibular division (V3) are responsible for sensation in the mid and lower parts of the face, respectively, and involvement in trigeminal neuralgia can cause hemifacial pain.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. 1: This nerve corresponds to the olfactory nerve (Cranial Nerve I), which is involved in the sense of smell, not relevant to the patient's symptoms.

 

Option B. 2: This nerve represents the optic nerve (Cranial Nerve II), which is responsible for vision and is not involved in the symptoms of facial pain and trigeminal neuralgia.

 

Option D. 4: This nerve corresponds to Cranial Nerve VI (Abducens nerve), responsible for eye movement (lateral rectus muscle), and is not related to the sensory complaints of this patient.

 

Educational objectives:

The patient's symptoms of facial pain, photophobia, and lacrimation suggest involvement of this nerve, while the normal reflexes rule out other cranial nerves such as the oculomotor nerve (Cranial Nerve III).

questions.stemHtml: Identify the papillae from the given histological section?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Circumvallate

 

The histological image shows a papilla with a circular appearance and a trench surrounding it. This characteristic trench on each side is a hallmark of the circumvallate papillae. These papillae are the largest of the tongue papillae and are arranged in a V-shaped pattern at the back of the tongue. They contain the largest number of taste buds and are primarily responsible for sensing taste.

 

The trench or moat-like structure around the circumvallate papilla helps trap dissolved food particles, allowing the taste buds to detect taste stimuli more effectively.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Fungiform: Fungiform papillae are mushroom-shaped and are smaller than circumvallate papillae. They are scattered across the surface of the tongue, especially at the tip and sides, and have a smooth surface without a trench-like structure.

 

Option C. Filiform: Filiform papillae are small, conical, and do not contain taste buds. They are responsible for the texture of the tongue and do not have the circular appearance or trenches seen in circumvallate papillae.

 

Option D. Foliate: Foliate papillae are leaf-like structures located on the lateral sides of the tongue. They appear as folds or ridges, not the circular appearance and trench seen in circumvallate papillae.

 

Educational objectives:

 

The circumvallate papillae are large, circular papillae located at the back of the tongue, surrounded by a trench, and contain a large number of taste buds. They are responsible for a significant portion of taste sensation.

questions.stem: Which of the following describes the movements known as pronation and supination?

options.label: A
options.text: The flexing of the arm with respect to the forearm around the elbow.

options.label: B
options.text: The elevation of the foot to the medial and lateral directions.

options.label: C
options.text: The twisting of the wrist while the elbow is held motionless.

options.label: D
options.text: The rotation at the shoulder that causes the arm to describe a cone shape.

questions.answerText: The twisting of the wrist while the elbow is held motionless.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) The twisting of the wrist while the elbow is held motionless.

 

Pronation and supination are movements that occur at the forearm, specifically at the superior and inferior radioulnar joints. These movements allow the twisting of the wrist with the elbow held motionless.

 

Supination refers to the outward rotation of the forearm, causing the palm to face upward.

 

Pronation refers to the inward rotation of the forearm, causing the palm to face downward.

 

These actions occur while keeping the elbow steady, involving the radius rotating over the ulna. 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. The flexing of the arm with respect to the forearm around the elbow: This describes flexion, which refers to bending the arm at the elbow, not pronation or supination.

 

Option B. The elevation of the foot to the medial and lateral directions: This describes movements like inversion and eversion of the foot, not pronation and supination of the forearm.

 

Option D. The rotation at the shoulder that causes the arm to describe a cone shape:  This refers to circumduction, which involves rotating the shoulder, not pronation or supination.

 

Educational objectives:

 

Pronation and supination refer to the twisting of the forearm (and consequently the wrist) while the elbow remains still. These movements allow the palm to face upward (supination) or downward (pronation).

questions.stem: A 32-year-old man presents to the clinic with complaints of weakness in his right arm after using crutches for six weeks. On examination, he has a deficit in the extension of his wrist and fingers, difficulty with thumb abduction, and diminished sense of touch over the posterior aspect of his arm, forearm, and dorsum of his hand. Which structure is most likely to be affected by the prolonged use of crutches?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Posterior cord

 

The patient's symptoms, including weakness in wrist and finger extension (wrist drop), difficulty with thumb abduction, and sensory loss over the posterior arm, forearm, and dorsum of the hand, indicate involvement of the radial nerve. The radial nerve is responsible for these motor and sensory functions, and it is a direct branch of the posterior cord of the brachial plexus.

 

Prolonged use of crutches, especially when they press into the axillary region (armpit), can compress the posterior cord, leading to radial nerve palsy. This condition is often referred to as "crutch palsy." The posterior cord gives rise to the radial and axillary nerves, both of which can be affected by this type of compression. The radial nerve innervates the extensor muscles of the forearm and provides sensory input to the areas affected in the patient.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Lateral cord: The lateral cord gives rise to the musculocutaneous nerve and contributes to the median nerve. Injury to this cord would primarily affect muscles involved in forearm flexion and general sensation in the lateral forearm, not the posterior arm or hand.

 

Option C. Medial cord: The medial cord gives rise to the ulnar nerve and also contributes to the median nerve. Its involvement would affect the muscles of the hand and sensation in the medial forearm and hand, but not the posterior arm and dorsum of the hand.

 

Option D. Upper trunk: The upper trunk forms from the union of the C5 and C6 nerve roots and contributes to the formation of the lateral and posterior cords. Injury to the upper trunk would cause weakness in the shoulder and biceps, but the sensory distribution described in the question points more directly to the radial nerve and posterior cord.

 

Educational objectives:

 

The posterior cord of the brachial plexus gives rise to the radial nerve, which is responsible for the extension of the wrist and fingers as well as sensation over the posterior arm, forearm, and dorsum of the hand. Prolonged use of crutches pressing into the axilla can lead to radial nerve compression and resulting symptoms such as wrist drop and sensory loss.

questions.stem: A 36-year-old auto driver was attacked and received a stab wound to the front of the neck. The wound was located on the right side, just lateral to the tip of the greater cornu of the hyoid bone. When asked to protrude his tongue, it deviated to the right. Which of the following statements is incorrect regarding the physical signs in this patient?

options.label: A
options.text: Paralysis of the right genioglossus muscle permitted the left genioglossus to pull the tongue forward and turned the tip to the right side

options.label: B
options.text: Genioglossus originates from the lower genial tubercles of the mandible

options.label: C
options.text: The hypoglossal nerve descends in the neck between the internal carotid artery and the internal jugular vein.

options.label: D
options.text: At about the level of the tip of the greater cornu of the hyoid bone the hypoglossal nerve turns forward and crosses the internal and external carotid arteries and the lingual artery to enter the tongue

questions.answerText: Genioglossus originates from the lower genial tubercles of the mandible
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Genioglossus originates from the lower genial tubercles of the mandible

 

The deviation of the tongue to the right when protruded indicates damage to the right hypoglossal nerve (Cranial Nerve XII), which innervates the genioglossus muscle on that side. The genioglossus muscle on the affected side is paralyzed, allowing the intact left genioglossus to pull the tongue towards the right (the weakened side).

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. The paralysis of the right genioglossus muscle leads to deviation of the tongue towards the affected side right: Because the left genioglossus pulls the tongue forward and turns the tip to the right. correct

 

Option C. The hypoglossal nerve does indeed descend between the internal carotid artery and the internal jugular vein: Before supplying the muscles of the tongue. correct

 

Option D. At about the level of the tip of the greater cornu of the hyoid bone, the hypoglossal nerve turns forward and crosses the internal and external carotid arteries and the lingual artery to enter the tongue: The hypoglossal nerve crosses several structures, including the internal and external carotid arteries and the lingual artery, at the level of the hyoid bone to supply the tongue muscles. correct

 

Educational objectives:

 

Injury to the hypoglossal nerve (Cranial Nerve XII) leads to tongue deviation towards the affected side due to unopposed action of the contralateral genioglossus muscle. The genioglossus muscle originates from the superior genial tubercles, not the lower ones.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy was brought to the hospital with multiple fractures of the humerus secondary to a fall from height. On examination, there is difficulty in flexion of the elbow and supination of the forearm, along with a loss of sensation over the lateral aspect of the forearm. Which nerve is most likely to be injured?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Musculocutaneous nerve

 

The clinical findings in this case—difficulty with elbow flexion, supination of the forearm, and loss of sensation over the lateral forearm—are consistent with injury to the musculocutaneous nerve.

 

The musculocutaneous nerve supplies:

 

  1. Biceps brachii, which is responsible for elbow flexion and acts as a powerful supinator of the forearm.
  2. Brachialis, which also contributes to elbow flexion.
  3. Coracobrachialis, which assists in flexion and adduction of the arm.

 

Musculocutaneous nerve provides sensory innervation to the lateral aspect of the forearm through its continuation as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm. The loss of sensation in this area supports musculocutaneous nerve involvement.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Median nerve: The median nerve is responsible for flexion of the wrist and fingers as well as pronation of the forearm. It does not innervate the muscles responsible for elbow flexion or supination, nor does it supply sensation to the lateral forearm.

 

Option B. Radial nerve: The radial nerve innervates the triceps (for elbow extension) and provides sensation to the posterior arm and forearm. While the radial nerve is associated with injuries to the humerus, particularly the shaft, the motor and sensory deficits in this case do not match radial nerve distribution.

 

Option D. Ulnar nerve: The ulnar nerve is responsible for fine motor control of the hand and supplies sensation to the medial side of the hand and forearm. It does not contribute to elbow flexion or supination and does not supply the lateral forearm.

 

Educational objectives:

 

The musculocutaneous nerve innervates the muscles responsible for elbow flexion and forearm supination (biceps brachii and brachialis) and provides sensation to the lateral forearm. In cases of injury, such as fractures of the humerus, the resulting motor and sensory deficits are characteristic of musculocutaneous nerve damage.

questions.stemHtml: Identify the sensory nerve supply for the given area of the hand?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Radial nerve

 

The image shows the dorsal aspect of the hand, specifically highlighting the area near the thumb, index finger, and middle finger. This area of the hand is primarily supplied by the radial nerve, which provides sensation to the dorsal surface of the thumb, index finger, middle finger, and part of the ring finger (except the tips of these fingers, which are innervated by the median nerve).

 

The radial nerve is responsible for sensory innervation of the dorsal part of the hand from the thumb to the midline of the ring finger, excluding the nail beds.

 

 

Educational objectives:

 

The radial nerve provides sensory innervation to the dorsal aspect of the hand, specifically covering the thumb, index, middle fingers, and part of the ring finger (excluding the fingertips). The median nerve supplies the nail beds and the palmar side of these fingers.

questions.stem: A 5-month-old girl was brought to the casualty with seizures. The pediatrician tries to perform a CSF sampling. What are the structures punctured by the pediatrician while piercing through the anterior fontanelle?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Scalp, dura, arachnoid

 

In a 5-month-old infant, the anterior fontanelle is still open, allowing direct access to the brain without having to pierce through the skull bones. When a pediatrician performs a CSF sampling through the anterior fontanelle, the needle will pass through the following layers:

 

  1. Scalp: The outermost layer.
  2. Dura mater: The outermost meningeal layer covering the brain.
  3. Arachnoid mater: The layer just beneath the dura mater.

 

Once the needle passes through these layers, it will reach the subarachnoid space where the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) is located.

 

The fontanelle itself is a gap in the skull where the bones have not yet fused, so no skull bone is pierced during the procedure.

 

Layers of scalp 

 

 

Educational objectives:

 

During CSF sampling through the anterior fontanelle, the needle passes through the scalp, dura mater, and arachnoid mater to access the subarachnoid space. There is no need to pierce any skull bone as the fontanelle is still open in infants.

questions.stemHtml: A 35-year-old male, diagnosed with squint, presented to the ophthalmology department for a regular checkup. On examination, a marked muscle was found affected. At which level does the nerve supply for the marked structure arise?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Red nucleus

 

The marked muscle in question is likely the medial rectus muscle, which is responsible for controlling eye movement towards the midline (adduction of the eye). The medial rectus muscle is innervated by the oculomotor nerve (Cranial Nerve III).

 

The oculomotor nerve arises from the oculomotor nucleus, which is located in the midbrain at the level of the red nucleus. This nerve controls most of the extraocular muscles, including the medial rectus muscle, and damage to this nerve can result in squint (strabismus) or other eye movement disorders.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Subthalamic nuclei: These nuclei are involved in motor control related to the basal ganglia, but they do not play a role in the innervation of the eye muscles.

 

Option C. Decussation of pyramidal tract: This refers to the crossing over of motor fibers in the medulla, which is involved in voluntary motor control of the limbs, not eye movements.

 

Option D. Olivary nucleus: This nucleus is part of the medulla oblongata and is involved in motor coordination, but it is not related to the oculomotor system or the eye muscles.

 

Educational objectives:

 

The oculomotor nerve (Cranial Nerve III), which innervates the medial rectus muscle, arises from the oculomotor nucleus in the midbrain, located at the level of the red nucleus. Damage to this nerve or its nucleus can lead to issues with eye movement, such as squints.

questions.stem: Which of the following are branches of the anterior division of the internal iliac artery? Superior gluteal arteryInferior gluteal arterySuperior vesical arteryMiddle rectal arteryInferior vesical arteryVaginal artery
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) 2, 3, 4, 5, 6

 

The internal iliac artery is divided into an anterior division and a posterior division, each giving rise to specific branches.

 

Branches of the anterior division of the internal iliac artery include:

 

2. Inferior gluteal artery:  Supplies the gluteal region.

 

3. Superior vesical artery:  Supplies the superior aspect of the bladder.

 

4. Middle rectal artery: Supplies the rectum.

 

5. Inferior vesical artery:  Supplies the inferior aspect of the bladder (in males, it also supplies the prostate and seminal vesicles).

 

6. Vaginal artery:  Equivalent to the inferior vesical artery in females, supplying the vagina and part of the bladder.

 

Other Options:

 

1. superior gluteal artery: is a branch of the posterior division of the internal iliac artery, which rules out choices that include it.

 

Educational objectives:

 

Branches of the anterior division of the internal iliac artery include the inferior gluteal artery, superior vesical artery, middle rectal artery, inferior vesical artery, and vaginal artery. The superior gluteal artery arises from the posterior division.

questions.stem: A patient, Vinod, who has taken the first COVID vaccine comes for the second dose. A nurse noticed that the shoulder was flabby, flat, and asymmetrical. There was an associated loss of contour of the shoulder joint. Injury to which of the structures might have resulted and was avoidable?

options.label: C
options.text: Lateral cutaneous nerve of the arm

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Deltoid muscle

 

Symptoms described—flabby shoulder, asymmetry, and loss of contour of the shoulder—are indicative of deltoid muscle atrophy. The deltoid muscle is essential for the rounded contour of the shoulder, and its weakness or atrophy would result in a flat appearance. The deltoid muscle is innervated by the axillary nerve, which is susceptible to injury, especially during intramuscular injections into the shoulder.

 

When an intramuscular injection is given improperly, particularly too high or posteriorly in the shoulder region, it can lead to damage of the axillary nerve. This nerve supplies the deltoid muscle, and damage to it can result in deltoid atrophy, loss of shoulder abduction, and weakness.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Rotator cuff: The rotator cuff is a group of muscles that stabilize the shoulder, but an injury to the rotator cuff would not cause the described flabby appearance or loss of shoulder contour.

 

Option B. Posterior circumflex artery: While this artery supplies the shoulder region, damage to it would cause vascular issues, not muscle atrophy.

 

Option C. Lateral cutaneous nerve of the arm: This nerve provides sensory innervation to the skin of the lateral arm. Damage to this nerve would cause sensory loss, not muscle atrophy.

 

Educational objectives:

 

Injections given improperly in the shoulder can damage the axillary nerve, leading to deltoid muscle atrophy, which results in a flat and asymmetrical shoulder appearance with a loss of its normal contour. The deltoid muscle plays a key role in the rounded shape of the shoulder and is vital for abduction of the arm.

questions.stemHtml: Fibers from the marked structure end in which of the following areas of the thalamus?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Anterior nucleus

 

The structure marked in the image is the mammillary body. The mammillary body is a part of the Papez circuit, which is involved in memory processing and emotional responses. Fibers from the mammillary body, known as the mammillothalamic tract, project to the anterior nucleus of the thalamus.

 

 

The Papez circuit connects several structures involved in memory, including the hippocampus, mammillary bodies, anterior nucleus of the thalamus, and the cingulate gyrus. The anterior nucleus of the thalamus receives input from the mammillary bodies and plays a crucial role in relaying information to the cingulate gyrus, ultimately contributing to memory formation.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Posterior nucleus: The posterior nucleus is not involved in the Papez circuit and does not receive fibers from the mammillary bodies.

 

Option B. Reticular nucleus: This nucleus is involved in regulating thalamocortical rhythms and sensory filtering but is unrelated to the mammillothalamic pathway.

 

Option D. Ventral lateral nucleus: This nucleus is involved in motor coordination and receives input from the cerebellum and basal ganglia, but it is not part of the Papez circuit.

 

Educational objectives:

 

The mammillary bodies send fibers through the mammillothalamic tract to the anterior nucleus of the thalamus, a key component of the Papez circuit, which plays a central role in memory processing.

questions.stem: A 75-year-old male presented with a history of frequency, hesitancy, and urgency for urination. He was on medication with Tamsulosin and Finasteride. Now, Trans Urethral Resection of Prostate (TURP) surgery was recommended by the physician. What is the volume of the prostate in normal adult males?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) 20cc

 

In a normal adult male, the typical volume of the prostate is approximately 20cc. The prostate tends to enlarge as men age, and conditions like benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) can lead to significant increases in size, which may require medical intervention or surgery, such as TURP (Trans Urethral Resection of Prostate).

 

BPH is common in older men and is characterized by symptoms like frequency, hesitancy, urgency, and weak urine stream. In this case, the patient is on Tamsulosin (an alpha-blocker that helps with muscle relaxation in the bladder neck) and Finasteride (a 5-alpha reductase inhibitor that helps reduce the size of the prostate). When medications fail to manage symptoms effectively, surgical interventions like TURP are recommended to relieve the blockage.

 

Educational objectives:

 

The normal prostate volume in adult males is approximately 20cc, and significant enlargement beyond this can lead to symptoms of BPH, potentially requiring treatment with medication or surgery, such as TURP.

questions.stemHtml: Which structure from the options given below is supplied by the nerve that arises from the marked area in the image?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Risorius

 

The image highlights the facial colliculus, which is an elevation on the dorsal aspect of the pons formed by the fibers of the facial nerve (Cranial Nerve VII) looping around the abducens nerve (Cranial Nerve VI). The facial nerve supplies the muscles of facial expression, including the risorius muscle, while the abducens nerve supplies the lateral rectus muscle.

 

The facial colliculus is primarily associated with the facial nerve's nucleus. Therefore, injury to the facial colliculus would affect the facial nerve first, leading to impairment of muscles responsible for facial expressions, such as the risorius. Though the abducens nerve, which supplies the lateral rectus, also passes through this area, the facial nerve is more superficial and therefore more likely to be affected.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Lateral rectus : This muscle is innervated by the abducens nerve (VI), which also passes near the facial colliculus. However, the facial nerve is more superficial and more likely to be impacted first.

 

Option B. Superior oblique: This muscle is innervated by the trochlear nerve (IV), which is not associated with the facial colliculus.

 

Option D. Levator palpebrae superioris: This muscle is innervated by the oculomotor nerve (III) and is unrelated to the facial colliculus.

 

Educational objectives:

 

The facial colliculus is closely associated with the facial nerve (VII) and the abducens nerve (VI). The risorius muscle is supplied by the facial nerve, which is more superficial and therefore more likely to be affected by damage to this area.

questions.stem: Which is not a branch of the facial artery?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Mental

 

The facial artery is a major branch of the external carotid artery, and it runs across the face, supplying various parts with blood. The primary branches of the facial artery include:

 

Lateral nasal: Supplies blood to the side of the nose.

 

Superior labial: Supplies blood to the upper lip.

 

Inferior labial: Supplies blood to the lower lip.

 

However, the mental artery is a branch of the inferior alveolar artery, not the facial artery. The inferior alveolar artery branches off the maxillary artery, which is a different artery altogether. This is why the mental artery is not a branch of the facial artery.

 

Educational objectives:

 

The mental artery is not a branch of the facial artery; it is a branch of the inferior alveolar artery.

questions.stem: Which of the following structures passing via the jugular foramen has a separate canal?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Glossopharyngeal nerve

 

The jugular foramen is an opening in the base of the skull through which several important structures pass. These structures are organized into different parts of the foramen:

 

Anterior part: Transmits the inferior petrosal sinus.

 

Posterior part: Transmits the internal jugular vein, a continuation of the sigmoid sinus.

 

Middle part: This portion transmits cranial nerves IX (Glossopharyngeal), X (Vagus), and XI (Accessory).

 

However, among these nerves, the glossopharyngeal nerve (IX) has its own dural sheath within the jugular foramen, distinguishing it from the vagus and accessory nerves, which share common pathways and structures as they pass through.

 

Other options:

 

Option A. Hypoglossal nerve: This nerve does not pass through the jugular foramen but instead travels through the hypoglossal canal.

 

Option C. Vagus nerve: The vagus nerve (X) passes through the jugular foramen, but it does not have a separate canal or dural sheath.

 

Option D. Accessory nerve: The accessory nerve (XI) also passes through the jugular foramen and shares the same passage as the vagus nerve without a separate canal.

 

Educational objectives:

 

The glossopharyngeal nerve (IX) has a separate canal within the jugular foramen, while the vagus and accessory nerves do not.

questions.stem: A young man presenting with features of recurrent brief depressive disorder, each lasting for about 3 to 7 days, for over a year. He had a history of occasional headaches and episodes of swooning attacks in between, usually precipitated by emotional events. His neuroimaging revealed agenesis of corpus callosum. He was experiencing swooning attacks as he became aware that some ‘unusual’ findings were present in his reports. Recurrent brief depression can be a manifestation of this congenital anomaly, and conversion disorder can be present as a comorbid diagnosis, perhaps due to ignorance and fear of this apparently innocuous congenital malformation. What is the blood supply of corpus callosum?

options.label: A
options.text: Anterior cerebral artery and middle cerebral artery

options.label: B
options.text: Anterior cerebral artery and posterior cerebral artery

options.label: C
options.text: Anterior cerebral artery and anterior communicating artery

options.label: D
options.text: Middle cerebral artery and posterior cerebral artery

questions.answerText: Anterior cerebral artery and anterior communicating artery
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Anterior cerebral artery and anterior communicating artery

 

 

Corpus callosum is the large bundle of nerve fibers that connects the two cerebral hemispheres, allowing communication between them. It is primarily supplied by the anterior cerebral artery (ACA), which branches off into smaller arteries like the pericallosal artery to supply the corpus callosum. The anterior communicating artery also plays a role in its blood supply by connecting the two ACAs and contributing to the vascularization of the midline structures, including the corpus callosum.

 

Other options:

 

Option A. Anterior cerebral artery and middle cerebral artery: The middle cerebral artery primarily supplies the lateral aspect of the brain, including the motor and sensory areas, and does not supply the corpus callosum, which is situated medially.

 

Option B. Anterior cerebral artery and posterior cerebral artery: While the ACA supplies most of the corpus callosum, the posterior cerebral artery (PCA) supplies the occipital lobe and inferior portions of the brain, but not the corpus callosum.

 

Option D. Middle cerebral artery and posterior cerebral artery: The middle cerebral artery, as discussed, does not contribute to the blood supply of the corpus callosum. The posterior cerebral artery does supply the posterior part, but without the involvement of the anterior cerebral artery, the blood supply would be incomplete.

 

Educational objectives:
 

The blood supply of the corpus callosum comes from the anterior cerebral artery and the posterior cerebral artery.

questions.stem: A patient age 45 presented with difficulty in foot eversion and sensory loss on the lateral leg and dorsum of the foot. The nerve injured is:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Superficial peroneal nerve

 

 

The superficial peroneal nerve is responsible for the motor innervation of the muscles that control foot eversion (specifically the peroneus longus and peroneus brevis). Additionally, this nerve provides sensory innervation to the skin over the lateral part of the leg and the dorsum of the foot, which corresponds to the sensory loss described in the patient. Injury to the superficial peroneal nerve would cause both motor and sensory deficits, as noted in the clinical presentation of difficulty with foot eversion and sensory loss on the lateral leg and dorsum of the foot.

 

Other options:

 

Option A. Deep peroneal nerve: The deep peroneal nerve primarily innervates the muscles of the anterior compartment of the leg, including the tibialis anterior, which are responsible for dorsiflexion of the foot. It provides sensory innervation to a small area between the first and second toes but does not supply the lateral leg or dorsum of the foot, so it is not the correct answer.

 

Option B. Sural nerve: The sural nerve provides sensory innervation to the posterior and lateral aspect of the lower leg and the lateral margin of the foot but does not innervate the muscles responsible for foot eversion, making this option incorrect.

 

Option D. Saphenous nerve: The saphenous nerve is a purely sensory nerve, supplying the medial aspect of the leg. It does not provide any motor function for foot eversion and does not innervate the lateral leg or dorsum of the foot, so this is also an incorrect option.

 

Educational objectives:
 

The superficial peroneal nerve is responsible for foot eversion and provides sensory innervation to the lateral leg and dorsum of the foot.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old lady, Janki, presented with loss of subconscious kinesthetic sensation, loss of pain and temperature sensation, as well as loss of crude touch from the body. On examination, fine touch sensation was found to be normal. In case of spinal angiography, blockage of which of the following arteries might be seen?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Anterior spinal artery


The symptoms described—loss of subconscious kinesthetic sensation, pain, temperature, and crude touch—are indicative of damage to the spinal tracts responsible for these sensations. The anterior spinal artery supplies the anterior two-thirds of the spinal cord, which includes the spinothalamic tracts responsible for pain, temperature, and crude touch, as well as the spinocerebellar tracts involved in subconscious kinesthetic sensation.

 

The anterior spinal artery syndrome is commonly associated with damage to these tracts, leading to the loss of the mentioned sensations, while sparing the dorsal columns, which are responsible for fine touch, vibration, and proprioception. This explains why fine touch remains intact in this patient.

 

Other options:

 

Option B. Posterior spinal artery: The posterior spinal artery primarily supplies the posterior third of the spinal cord, which includes the dorsal columns. Damage to the posterior spinal artery typically results in the loss of fine touch, vibration, and proprioception, but this patient still has fine touch intact, making this an incorrect option.

 

Option C. Anterior inferior cerebellar artery: The anterior inferior cerebellar artery (AICA) supplies parts of the cerebellum and the brainstem but does not supply the spinal cord. Therefore, this option is incorrect in the context of spinal cord pathology.

 

Option D. Posterior inferior cerebellar artery: The posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) supplies parts of the cerebellum and brainstem, but like the AICA, it does not supply the spinal cord. This makes it an incorrect option for the current presentation.

 

Educational objectives:
 

The anterior spinal artery supplies the anterior two-thirds of the spinal cord, including the spinothalamic and spinocerebellar tracts. Blockage of this artery results in loss of pain, temperature, crude touch, and subconscious kinesthetic sensation, while fine touch is spared.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old female, Vimla, presented after a road traffic accident with a brief loss of consciousness. On general examination, she exhibited fatigue, pallor, and weakness. She also had mild jaundice and gallstones, with massive hepatosplenomegaly and hypersplenism. Skull radiography revealed widening of the diploic spaces. Her medical history includes failure to thrive in early childhood, growth retardation, delayed puberty, leg ulcers, and skin bronzing. Following the accident, she now has a headache, lucid interval, nausea, vomiting, and focal neurological deficits. Plain X-ray shows a skull fracture, and a CT scan reveals hyperdense biconvex opacity in the temporal region. What is your single best diagnosis for the current presentation?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Extradural haemorrhage


symptom indicating extradural hemorrhage (also known as epidural hematoma) is the presence of a lucid interval following the initial brief loss of consciousness. This pattern is characteristic of an extradural hemorrhage, where there is a temporary recovery in consciousness followed by a gradual neurological decline. The hyperdense biconvex opacity on the CT scan in the temporal region is also typical of extradural hemorrhage, where blood accumulates between the dura mater and the skull, often due to a skull fracture, which is also present in this patient.

 

The patient’s history of jaundice, hepatosplenomegaly, gallstones, and widening of the diploic spaces are consistent with a chronic condition like thalassemia, a blood disorder causing bone marrow expansion and leading to skeletal abnormalities. However, her current presentation after the road traffic accident, particularly the skull fracture and lucid interval, points directly to an extradural hemorrhage rather than the underlying chronic condition.

 

Other options:

 

Option A. Thalassemia: Although the patient has multiple signs consistent with thalassemia (e.g., hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice, gallstones, and widened diploic spaces), the acute neurological symptoms following the head injury, such as the lucid interval and findings on CT, are more indicative of extradural hemorrhage.

 

Option B. Migraine: The patient's symptoms, especially the lucid interval, skull fracture, and CT findings, are not consistent with a migraine. Migraines do not typically present with such findings after trauma, making this an incorrect option.

 

Option C. Subarachnoid hemorrhage: Subarachnoid hemorrhage typically presents with a "thunderclap" headache, described as the worst headache of a patient’s life. In this case, the patient’s headache and neurological deficits are associated with a lucid interval, which is more characteristic of an extradural hemorrhage. Furthermore, a subarachnoid hemorrhage would not present with a hyperdense biconvex opacity on CT scan.

 

Educational objectives:


Extradural hemorrhage is associated with a lucid interval following trauma, and CT imaging typically shows a hyperdense biconvex opacity. It is often caused by a skull fracture, as seen in this patient.

questions.stem: A patient, Ramlal, a 56-year-old male, presented with a history of palanaesthesia, astereognosis, loss of proprioception, and loss of fine touch sensation. He has a chronic history of smoking, diabetes, and hypertension. In the case of spinal angiography, blockage of which of the following arteries might be seen?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Posterior spinal artery


The posterior spinal artery supplies the dorsal columns of the spinal cord, which are responsible for proprioception, fine touch, and vibration sensation. Damage to the dorsal columns leads to symptoms such as palanaesthesia (loss of tactile sensation), astereognosis (inability to recognize objects by touch), and loss of proprioception and fine touch, as seen in this patient. The chronic history of smoking, diabetes, and hypertension increases the risk of vascular damage, which can lead to blockage of the posterior spinal artery.

 

The posterior spinal artery is the primary vessel responsible for supplying the posterior one-third of the spinal cord, which includes the dorsal columns. Blockage of this artery would explain the sensory deficits, particularly the loss of fine touch and proprioception, without affecting motor function.

 

Other options:

 

Option A. Anterior spinal artery: The anterior spinal artery supplies the anterior two-thirds of the spinal cord, including the spinothalamic tract and corticospinal tract, which are responsible for pain, temperature, and motor control. Since the patient is primarily experiencing sensory deficits related to fine touch and proprioception, the anterior spinal artery is not the correct answer.

 

Option C. Anterior inferior cerebellar artery: The anterior inferior cerebellar artery supplies the cerebellum and part of the brainstem, but it does not supply the spinal cord. Therefore, this artery is unrelated to the symptoms described and is not the correct choice.

 

Option D. Posterior inferior cerebellar artery: The posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) supplies the cerebellum and part of the brainstem, but like the anterior inferior cerebellar artery, it does not supply the spinal cord. This makes it an incorrect option for this presentation.

 

Educational objectives:


The posterior spinal artery supplies the dorsal columns of the spinal cord, which are responsible for fine touch, proprioception, and vibration sensation. Blockage of this artery leads to sensory deficits, such as loss of proprioception and fine touch, while sparing motor function.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old male, Jagan, presented with severe headache, vomiting, and a history of immediate unconsciousness. On admission, he was found hypertensive with a history of poorly controlled hypertension. Gradual decline in neurological functions was noted. Neck stiffness and a positive Kernig’s sign were found. An NCCT scan failed to make a diagnosis. A lumbar puncture (LP) revealed grossly bloody cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) with RBC counts up to 1 million/cu mm. After 48 hours, xanthochromic spinal fluid was found. What is your single best diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Subarachnoid haemorrhage


The presentation of sudden severe headache (often described as "the worst headache of my life"), vomiting, and immediate unconsciousness strongly suggests a subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH). This is further supported by the positive Kernig’s sign and neck stiffness, which indicate meningeal irritation—a common finding in SAH.

 

The lumbar puncture showing grossly bloody CSF with elevated RBC counts, followed by the appearance of xanthochromic spinal fluid after 48 hours, confirms the diagnosis of SAH. Xanthochromia occurs when red blood cells in the CSF break down, causing a yellow discoloration that is a classic sign of SAH.

 

Hypertension, especially when poorly controlled, is a significant risk factor for subarachnoid hemorrhage due to the increased likelihood of cerebral aneurysm rupture or other vascular pathology leading to bleeding in the subarachnoid space.

 

Other options:

 

Option A. Meningitis: Meningitis can cause neck stiffness and Kernig’s sign but typically presents with fever and is not associated with grossly bloody CSF. The presence of bloody CSF and xanthochromia points away from meningitis and towards a hemorrhagic event like SAH.

 

Option B. Intracerebral haemorrhage: While intracerebral hemorrhage can present with sudden neurological symptoms, it is not typically associated with grossly bloody CSF and xanthochromia. Intracerebral hemorrhage often shows focal neurological deficits, whereas SAH leads to more generalized meningeal irritation.

 

Option D. Extradural haemorrhage: Extradural hemorrhage is usually associated with a history of trauma and presents with a "lucid interval" where the patient initially regains consciousness after injury before deteriorating again. It is not commonly associated with bloody CSF or xanthochromia, making this an unlikely diagnosis.

 

Educational objectives:


Subarachnoid hemorrhage presents with sudden, severe headache, unconsciousness, and meningeal signs. The lumbar puncture showing grossly bloody CSF and xanthochromia after 48 hours confirms the diagnosis.

questions.stem: In adults, lumbar puncture is done at?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) L3-L4


In adults, a lumbar puncture is typically performed between the L3-L4 vertebrae. This location is chosen because the spinal cord usually ends at the level of L1 in adults. Performing the procedure below this level minimizes the risk of damaging the spinal cord. The lumbar puncture involves inserting a needle into the subarachnoid space to collect cerebrospinal fluid or to administer medications, and the L3-L4 interspace is commonly used as it is well below the termination of the spinal cord, providing a safer site for this procedure.

 

Educational objectives:


In adults, lumbar puncture is typically performed at the L3-L4 level because the spinal cord ends at the L1 level, making this a safe site to avoid injury to the spinal cord.

 

In Children, lumbar puncture is done at L4-L5

questions.stem: A 35-year-old alcoholic and chronic smoker male, Amit, with a history of hypercholesterolemia for 8 years, presented to the OPD with hemiplegia on the right side of his body. On examination, he had loss of proprioception, fine touch, and vibration sensations on the right side. He was also unable to recognize objects with his right hand when his eyes were closed (astereognosis). On further examination, his tongue was found to be atrophied on the left side with deviation to the left upon protrusion. Cerebral angiography revealed blockage of an artery located in the median fissure of the spinal cord at the lower part of the brainstem. What is your diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Dejerine’s syndrome

 

Dejerine’s syndrome, also known as medial medullary syndrome, results from the occlusion of the anterior spinal artery or paramedian branches of the vertebral arteries, which supply the medial part of the medulla. This condition leads to a characteristic triad of symptoms:

 

  1. Contralateral hemiplegia due to involvement of the corticospinal tract.
  2. Contralateral loss of proprioception, vibration, and fine touch due to damage to the medial lemniscus.
  3. Ipsilateral hypoglossal nerve palsy (cranial nerve XII), causing tongue atrophy and deviation toward the side of the lesion.

 

Amit's symptoms of hemiplegia on the right side, loss of proprioception, fine touch, and vibration on the right side, along with atrophy and deviation of the tongue to the left side, strongly indicate medial medullary syndrome (Dejerine's syndrome). The blockage found in the median fissure at the lower part of the brainstem, which supplies the medulla, 

 

Other options:

 

Option A. Perinaud’s syndrome: Perinaud’s syndrome is a dorsal midbrain syndrome typically involving vertical gaze palsy and is not associated with the symptoms seen in this case, such as hemiplegia, loss of proprioception, or tongue deviation.

 

Option B. Benedikt’s syndrome: Benedikt’s syndrome results from a lesion in the midbrain and involves contralateral hemiparesis and ipsilateral oculomotor nerve (cranial nerve III) palsy. The involvement of the hypoglossal nerve and the lower brainstem is not characteristic of Benedikt's syndrome, making it an incorrect choice.

 

Option D. Wallenberg syndrome: Wallenberg syndrome (lateral medullary syndrome) is caused by occlusion of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) or vertebral arteries, affecting the lateral part of the medulla. Symptoms typically include ipsilateral loss of pain and temperature sensation on the face, contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation on the body, and cranial nerve X dysfunction (dysphagia, hoarseness). There is no involvement of the corticospinal tract or the hypoglossal nerve, making it an incorrect diagnosis in this case.

 

Educational objectives:


Dejerine’s syndrome, or medial medullary syndrome, is caused by blockage of the anterior spinal artery and involves contralateral hemiplegia, contralateral loss of proprioception, fine touch, and vibration, along with ipsilateral hypoglossal nerve palsy, leading to tongue atrophy and deviation.

questions.stem: Handlebar palsy occurs due to compression of which nerve?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Ulnar nerve

 

 

Handlebar palsy occurs due to prolonged pressure or compression of the ulnar nerve at the wrist, specifically at the Guyon’s canal, which is located near the hypothenar eminence. This type of nerve injury is commonly seen in cyclists who maintain a forward-tilting posture with their hands gripping the handlebar, leading to direct compression of the ulnar nerve. The ulnar nerve supplies sensation to the ring and little fingers and controls the small muscles of the hand. Compression leads to symptoms like tingling, numbness, or weakness in these areas.

 

Other options:

 

Option A. Median nerve: The median nerve runs through the carpal tunnel and is primarily involved in carpal tunnel syndrome, not handlebar palsy. Compression of the median nerve affects the thumb, index, middle fingers, and part of the ring finger.

 

Option C. Radial nerve: The radial nerve is responsible for motor control of the posterior arm and forearm, and its compression leads to wrist drop, not handlebar palsy.

 

Option D. Axillary nerve: The axillary nerve supplies the deltoid and teres minor muscles and does not run near the wrist or hand. Its compression would not lead to the symptoms seen in handlebar palsy.

 

Educational objectives:


Handlebar palsy is caused by compression of the ulnar nerve, often due to prolonged pressure on the hypothenar eminence while gripping a handlebar during cycling.

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Nerve in Pterygoid canal

 

 

The Vidian nerve, also known as the nerve of the pterygoid canal, is formed by the union of the greater superficial petrosal nerve (carrying parasympathetic fibers) and the deep petrosal nerve (carrying sympathetic fibers). It runs through the pterygoid canal, and Vidian’s neurectomy involves cutting this nerve to reduce symptoms such as chronic rhinitis by decreasing the parasympathetic innervation to the nasal mucosa.

 

Other options:

Option C. Nerve in Tympanomastoid fissure: This refers to the nerves in the region of the tympanomastoid fissure, such as the auricular branch of the vagus nerve, which is not related to Vidian's nerve or its function.

questions.stemHtml: Blockage of the artery supplying the indicated area will cause all except?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Ataxia

 

The area indicated by the arrow in the image is the paracentral lobule. The paracentral lobule is located in the medial portion of the brain and controls motor and sensory functions for the lower extremities and the perineal region, including the rectum and bladder. This region is supplied by the anterior cerebral artery (ACA).

 

Ataxia is not associated with this region but is typically caused by damage to the cerebellum, which controls balance and coordination. Since the cerebellum is not supplied by the anterior cerebral artery, ataxia would not be a result of a blockage in this area.

 

Other Options

Option B. Urinary incontinence: The same region controls bladder function.

 

Option C. Perianal anaesthesia: Sensory loss in the perineum can occur with damage to the paracentral lobule.

 

Educational objectives:


Blockage of the artery supplying the paracentral lobule (anterior cerebral artery) can lead to incontinence and sensory loss in the perineal region but does not result in ataxia, which is associated with cerebellar damage.

The anterior communicating artery, internal carotid artery (ICA), infundibulum (pituitary stalk), posterior communicating artery, and oculomotor (III) and trochlear (IV) nerves are important anatomical structures involved in the Circle of Willis and cranial nerve pathways
