Ans. B) Adductor pollicis


The adductor pollicis is often referred to as the "graveyard" of the ulnar nerve because this is the terminal muscle that the ulnar nerve innervates in the hand. The ulnar nerve is responsible for supplying most of the intrinsic hand muscles, and the adductor pollicis is one of the most important muscles it controls, involved in thumb adduction.

 

Most of the thenar muscles (related to thumb movement) are supplied by the median nerve, except for the adductor pollicis, which is exclusively supplied by the ulnar nerve.

 

Other options:

Option C. Extensor pollicis longus: This muscle extends the thumb and is also innervated by the radial nerve, not the ulnar nerve.

 

Option D. Extensor pollicis brevis: This muscle extends the thumb and is innervated by the radial nerve, not the ulnar nerve.

 

Educational objectives:


The adductor pollicis is the last muscle innervated by the ulnar nerve in the hand, making it the "graveyard" of the ulnar nerve.

questions.stemHtml: Identify the vertebra.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) C1


The vertebra shown in the image is the C1 vertebra, also known as the atlas. The C1 vertebra is unique because it lacks a vertebral body and a spinous process, distinguishing it from other cervical vertebrae. Instead, it has an anterior and posterior arch forming a ring-like structure, which supports the skull and allows for the nodding motion of the head. The presence of the large foramen transversarium (transverse foramen) is another key feature, indicating that it is a cervical vertebra.

 

The atlas articulates with the occipital condyles of the skull and the C2 vertebra (axis), allowing for a wide range of head movements.

 

Other options:

 

Option B. C2: The C2 vertebra, also known as the axis, has a distinctive odontoid process (dens) that projects upward and forms a pivot for the rotation of the atlas and skull. This feature is absent in the vertebra shown in the image.

 

Option C, D. C3 and D) C4: Both C3 and C4 are typical cervical vertebrae that possess a vertebral body and a spinous process, which are not present in the atlas (C1). Hence, these are incorrect.

 

Educational objectives:
 

The C1 vertebra (atlas) is a ring-shaped vertebra without a body or spinous process, allowing it to support and articulate with the skull. It is essential for head movement, and its unique structure differentiates it from other cervical vertebrae.

questions.stemHtml: Identify the Honeymoon muscle.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) A

 

 

The muscle labeled A in the image is the sartorius muscle, commonly referred to as the "Honeymoon muscle." The sartorius is the longest muscle in the body and runs obliquely across the anterior thigh, originating from the anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) and inserting on the medial side of the tibia. It is involved in flexion, abduction, and lateral rotation of the thigh at the hip joint and flexion of the knee.

 

Other options:

 

Option B. B: This is the rectus femoris, part of the quadriceps group, which is responsible for knee extension and hip flexion.

 

Option C. C: This is the vastus lateralis, another muscle of the quadriceps group, involved in extending the knee.

 

Option D. D: This is the gracilis, a muscle of the medial thigh, which is involved in adducting the thigh and assisting in flexion and medial rotation of the knee.

 

Educational objectives:
 

The sartorius muscle is the "Honeymoon muscle," known for its unique oblique path across the thigh and involvement in multiple movements of the hip and knee.

questions.stemHtml: A 48-year-old female patient presented with recurrent episodes of severe abdominal pain, which is often accompanied by nausea and vomiting. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy reveals multiple peptic ulcers in the duodenal bulb. Laboratory tests show elevated gastrin levels. She was given Prilosec for a long time. She was also consuming a vegetarian diet and now presented with tiredness & palpitations for a month. She complained of progressive sensory loss in her lower extremities. Neurological examination reveals impaired vibratory sensation in both legs. An MRI of the spinal cord shows no structural abnormalities. On blood examination, she had the following hematological slide. All of the following statements are correct in this case except:

options.label: A
options.text: This is a case of gastrinoma with high gastrin secretion resulting in hypersecretion of hydrochloric acid.

options.label: B
options.text: Prilosec is an example of a proton pump inhibitor which may cause decreased Vit B12 absorption.

options.label: C
options.text: In this patient, due to Vitamin B12 deficiency, myelination of the anterior spinothalamic tract has been affected.

options.label: D
options.text: On hematological examination, increased mean corpuscular volume (MCV, >100 fL) and mean corpuscular hemoglobin (MCH) and polymorphonuclear cells with multiple lobes are found.

questions.answerText: In this patient, due to Vitamin B12 deficiency, myelination of the anterior spinothalamic tract has been affected.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) In this patient, due to Vitamin B12 deficiency, myelination of the anterior spinothalamic tract has been affected.


In cases of Vitamin B12 deficiency, the spinal cord's posterior columns (fasciculus gracilis and fasciculus cuneatus) are affected, leading to impaired proprioception and vibration sense. These tracts are responsible for carrying proprioceptive and fine touch information. The anterior spinothalamic tract, which is responsible for pain and temperature sensation, is not typically affected by B12 deficiency. 

 

Other options:


Option A. This is a case of gastrinoma with high gastrin secretion resulting in hypersecretion of hydrochloric acid: This statement is correct. The patient’s elevated gastrin levels and multiple peptic ulcers are consistent with a diagnosis of gastrinoma (Zollinger-Ellison syndrome), which leads to excessive secretion of hydrochloric acid, causing ulcers.

 

Option B. Prilosec is an example of a proton pump inhibitor which may cause decreased Vit B12 absorption: This statement is correct. Long-term use of proton pump inhibitors like Prilosec (omeprazole) can reduce stomach acid, which is necessary for the absorption of Vitamin B12. This can lead to a deficiency over time, especially in patients on a vegetarian diet.

 

Option D. On hematological examination, increased mean corpuscular volume (MCV, >100 fL) and mean corpuscular hemoglobin (MCH) and polymorphonuclear cells with multiple lobes are found: This statement is correct. The patient’s blood smear reveals hypersegmented neutrophils, which are typical in megaloblastic anemia, a condition commonly caused by Vitamin B12 deficiency. Elevated MCV and MCH also point towards macrocytic anemia, another feature of B12 deficiency.

 

Educational objectives:


Vitamin B12 deficiency causes subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord, primarily affecting the posterior columns, not the anterior spinothalamic tract.

questions.stemHtml: A 61-year-old male presents to the neurology clinic with a complaint of tremors and difficulty with movement. He reports that over the past year, he has noticed a gradual slowing down of his movements, stiffness in his limbs, and a persistent tremor in his right hand. His family members have also observed that his handwriting has become smaller and less legible. Additionally, he has experienced some balance problems and has had several falls in the last few months. On further inquiry, he mentions that he occasionally experiences a shuffling gait and finds it challenging to initiate and sustain his walking. Deficiency in synthesis of a particular neurotransmitter leads to this situation. This particular neurotransmitter is produced in which of the sites marked below?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) B


symptoms—tremors, bradykinesia (slowness of movement), rigidity, and shuffling gait—are characteristic of Parkinson’s disease. Parkinson’s disease results from the degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra, a structure located in the midbrain. The loss of dopamine production in this area leads to the motor deficits seen in Parkinson’s disease.

 

In the image provided, B marks the substantia nigra, which is the site of dopamine production. Degeneration of the neurons in this region leads to a reduction in dopamine levels and the characteristic symptoms of Parkinson's disease.

 

 

Other options:

 

Option A. Corpus callosum: which connects the left and right hemispheres of the brain. It is not involved in dopamine production.

 

Option C.  Pons:  which is part of the brainstem and involved in relaying signals between the cerebrum and cerebellum. It does not produce dopamine.

 

Option D. Medulla oblongata: which controls autonomic functions such as breathing and heart rate but is not involved in dopamine synthesis.

 

Educational objectives:
 

The substantia nigra, located in the midbrain, is the site of dopamine production. Degeneration of this area is responsible for the motor symptoms seen in Parkinson’s disease.

questions.stemHtml: A 23-year-old female presents to the emergency room with complaints of severe headaches and visual disturbances for the past week. She describes the headaches as throbbing in nature, located mainly around her temples and forehead. The visual disturbances include blurred vision and seeing "flashing lights" in her peripheral vision. She has no significant medical history but mentions that her brother has a history of similar symptoms. On detailed neurological examination, bilateral papilledema was observed on fundoscopic examination. Further evaluation, including neuroimaging, confirms the presence of an intracranial mass. The radiologist takes measurements and identifies the location of the mass relative to the patient's skull using a reference point known as Frankfurt’s plane. This plane passes through?

options.label: A
options.text: Supraorbital margin and upper margin of external acoustic meatus

options.label: B
options.text: Supraorbital margin and lower margin of external acoustic meatus

options.label: C
options.text: Infraorbital margin and upper margin of external acoustic meatus

options.label: D
options.text: Infraorbital margin and lower margin of external acoustic meatus

questions.answerText: Infraorbital margin and upper margin of external acoustic meatus
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Infraorbital margin and upper margin of external acoustic meatus

 

The Frankfurt plane (Frankfort horizontal plane) is an anatomical reference plane used in radiology and anthropometry. It passes through two specific points on the skull:

 

The infraorbital margin (the lower border of the orbit).

 

The upper margin of the external acoustic meatus (the superior edge of the ear canal).

 

This plane is significant because it aligns the skull in a standardized position, which is especially useful for accurate measurements in imaging studies. The Frankfurt plane is often used in neuroimaging to help locate intracranial masses or other abnormalities in relation to the skull.

 

Educational objectives:

 

The Frankfurt plane passes through the infraorbital margin and the upper margin of the external acoustic meatus, and is used in radiology and imaging for precise positioning and measurement.

questions.stemHtml: A 35-year-old male presents to the orthopedic clinic with complaints of shoulder pain and weakness in his right arm for the past several weeks. He reports that the pain is most severe when he tries to lift objects or reach overhead. Physical examination reveals tenderness in the anterior aspect of the shoulder, and the patient demonstrates weakness in flexing his right arm against resistance. Which structure is having the highest probability to be affected in this case?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) C


The patient describes shoulder pain and weakness when lifting objects or reaching overhead, along with weakness in arm flexion. These symptoms suggest involvement of the biceps brachii muscle, particularly its short head, which is responsible for flexion of the shoulder and elbow. The short head of the biceps originates from the coracoid process of the scapula 

 

The biceps brachii plays a significant role in shoulder flexion, and the patient's symptoms point towards this muscle being affected. Flexion against resistance becoming painful or weak indicates a potential problem with this muscle.

 

Other options:

 

Option A. Deltoid: The deltoid muscle is involved in shoulder abduction, particularly during the early phases. It is less involved in flexion, and although it could contribute to overhead pain, it is not the main muscle affected in flexion-based movements.

 

Option B. Coracoacromial ligament: This ligament stabilizes the shoulder joint but is not directly involved in arm flexion. It connects the coracoid process to the acromion and prevents upward displacement of the humerus. While it supports shoulder stability, it would not primarily cause weakness in flexion.

 

Option D. Short head of the biceps brachii: This is closely associated with C, as it originates from the coracoid process. While D refers to the short head itself, C (coracoid process) marks the origin point where the biceps attaches. In this context, C is the better choice to represent the issue affecting the biceps.

questions.stemHtml: A 42-year-old male presents to the emergency department with diplopia. Neurological examination reveals that he has difficulty in looking upward. On radiological examination, a mass was found on the dorsum of the brain, which was compressing a nearby structure. Which of the following statements is true in this patient?

options.label: A
options.text: Most probably this patient is presenting with a tumour of B, which is causing compression of A, resulting in downward gaze.

options.label: B
options.text: Most probably this patient is presenting with a tumour of C, which is causing compression of B, resulting in downward gaze.

options.label: C
options.text: Most probably this patient is presenting with a tumour of B, which is causing compression of C, resulting in downward gaze.

options.label: D
options.text: Most probably this patient is presenting with a tumour of A, which is causing compression of B, resulting in downward gaze.

questions.answerText: Most probably this patient is presenting with a tumour of A, which is causing compression of B, resulting in downward gaze.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Most probably this patient is presenting with a tumor of A, which is causing compression of B, resulting in downward gaze.

 

The patient presents with diplopia and difficulty looking upward. This indicates an issue with the upward gaze control, which is mediated by the superior colliculus located in the midbrain. The superior colliculus is responsible for coordinating eye movements, particularly upward gaze.

 

In this case, a pineal gland tumour (marked as A) is causing compression of the superior colliculus (marked as B), which leads to difficulty in upward gaze. Compression of this area can cause Parinaud’s syndrome, a condition characterized by paralysis of upward gaze. This syndrome occurs due to compression of the tectal plate, specifically the superior colliculus, by the tumour of the pineal gland.

 

Other options:

 

Option A. Most probably this patient is presenting with a tumor of B, which is causing compression of A, resulting in downward gaze: This option incorrectly states that the tumor is of the superior colliculus (B) and that it is compressing the pineal gland (A). However, the pineal gland is not responsible for eye movements, and the superior colliculus is the structure being compressed, not causing the compression.

 

Option B. Most probably this patient is presenting with a tumor of C, which is causing compression of B, resulting in downward gaze: This option suggests a tumor of the inferior colliculus (C) is compressing the superior colliculus (B), which would be incorrect as the inferior colliculus does not typically cause the symptoms described in this patient. The superior colliculus controls upward gaze, not the inferior colliculus.

 

Option C. Most probably this patient is presenting with a tumor of B, which is causing compression of C, resulting in downward gaze: A tumor of the superior colliculus (B) compressing the inferior colliculus (C) would not lead to upward gaze problems. Instead, the symptoms are due to compression of the superior colliculus by a tumor of the pineal gland (A).

 

Educational objectives:



Parinaud’s syndrome results from compression of the superior colliculus by a pineal gland tumor, leading to problems with upward gaze.

questions.stemHtml: A 61-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with a complaint of a painful lump in her right groin that has been gradually increasing in size over the past few weeks. She describes the pain as constant and sharp, exacerbated when she coughs or strains. The patient has a history of multiple pregnancies and has noticed a bulge in her groin area when lifting heavy objects. On examination, there is a tender, firm, and irreducible mass in the right femoral region just below the inguinal ligament. The overlying skin appears erythematous. The patient's vital signs are stable. Proper diagnosis was made with all clinical examination and surgical treatment was decided. During this surgery, it became very important to identify the pectineal ligament, lacunar ligament, and inguinal ligament. Identify the ligaments in the image:

options.label: A
options.text: A-Inguinal ligament, B-lacunar ligament, C-Pectineal ligament

options.label: B
options.text: A-Lacunar ligament, B-Inguinal ligament, C-Pectineal ligament

options.label: C
options.text: A-Pectineal ligament, B-Inguinal ligament, C-Lacunar ligament

options.label: D
options.text: A-Inguinal ligament, B-Pectineal ligament, C-Lacunar ligament

questions.answerText: A-Inguinal ligament, B-Pectineal ligament, C-Lacunar ligament
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) A-Inguinal ligament, B-Pectineal ligament, C-Lacunar ligament

 

During the surgical procedure to address the patient's femoral hernia, it is essential to correctly identify the ligaments in the inguinal region for successful repair.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. A-Inguinal ligament: which extends from the anterior superior iliac spine to the pubic tubercle, forming the upper boundary of the femoral canal.

 

Option B. A-Pectineal ligament: which runs along the pecten pubis and is essential for surgical procedures in the lower abdominal region.

 

Option C. A- Lacunar ligament: located medially, connecting to the pectineal ligament and aiding in defining the medial boundary of the femoral canal.

The inguinal ligament forms the superior boundary of the femoral canal, while the lacunar ligament lies medially, and the pectineal ligament runs along the pecten pubis. These ligaments are critical landmarks in surgeries addressing groin hernias.

questions.stemHtml: A 30-year-old woman presents to her obstetrician for a routine prenatal check-up during her first trimester of pregnancy. She is eager to learn about the development of her growing fetus and asks about the early stages of spinal cord formation. The obstetrician explains that during the early 6th week of embryonic life, significant developmental events occur in the cervical region of the spinal cord. These events involve the notochord, a critical structure in embryonic development. Identify the position of the different structures in the image below:

options.label: A
options.text: A - dorsal root ganglion, B – dorsal root of spinal nerve, C – notochord, D – trunk of spinal nerve

options.label: B
options.text: A - ventral root of spinal nerve, B – dorsal root ganglion, C – notochord, D – trunk of spinal nerve

options.label: C

questions.answerText: A - dorsal root of spinal nerve, B – ventral root of spinal nerve, C – notochord, D – trunk of spinal nerve
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) A - dorsal root of spinal nerve, B – ventral root of spinal nerve, C – notochord, D – trunk of spinal nerve

 

The image represents an early embryonic stage of the spinal cord development, a process occurring during the 6th week of gestation. The neural tube, which later differentiates into the spinal cord, is visible. Several key structures can be identified in the cross-section of the developing neural tissue:

 

dorsal and ventral roots come together to form a mixed nerve that carries both sensory and motor information.

 

Option A. Is the dorsal root of the spinal nerve, which carries sensory information from the peripheral nerves to the spinal cord. The dorsal roots are primarily responsible for transmitting afferent (sensory) signals.

 

Option B. Ventral root of the spinal nerve, which carries motor commands from the spinal cord to the muscles. This structure is crucial in transmitting efferent (motor) signals.

 

Option C. Notochord: a primitive structure crucial for the early development of the axial skeleton. The notochord serves as a signaling center that influences the formation of the surrounding tissues, including the vertebrae and the neural tube.

In the early stages of spinal cord development, the dorsal root of the spinal nerve transmits sensory information, while the ventral root carries motor signals. questions.stemHtml: A patient was presented with exacerbated chronic lower back pain in the sacral region with irradiation to the back of the left leg, producing strong throbbing and burning pain behind the knee. Pain was aggravated when bending forward or reaching out. In his history, he had a back condition from birth and later had an accident that resulted in a fracture of the lumbar vertebrae. His MRI two months prior to this aggravation showed degeneration of L1, disc degeneration, and protrusion of the disc at the S1 level. He was prescribed strong non-steroidal pain medication that made him feel drowsy, but did not provide full pain relief. Seeking resolution for his pain, he decided to try InterX therapy and treatment was aimed at the whole lumbar-sacral zone, dermatomes L1/L2 and L4, L5, S1–S3, left buttock, right buttock, and left back of the knee. After two and a half weeks of use, he reported no pain or discomfort, stopped taking pain medication, and started a core exercise program to stabilize the lumbar spine. Six months of follow-up confirmed that the patient remained pain-free, actively working, and traveling.All of the following anatomical statements are true about this case except:

options.label: A
options.text: A & D arise from the same bony point.

options.label: B
options.text: C runs in between the vein and nerve.

options.label: C
options.text: B is affected in this case due to which all symptoms appeared.

questions.answerText: C runs in between the vein and nerve.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) C runs in between the vein and nerve.

 

This case describes a patient with sciatica, which is characterized by chronic lower back pain radiating to the leg, typically due to compression of the sciatic nerve. The sciatic nerve (B) is the largest nerve in the body and originates from the lumbar and sacral spinal nerves. The pain described in this case is due to the compression of the sciatic nerve, which is confirmed by the patient's MRI findings showing disc degeneration at the S1 level. The cadaveric image highlights relevant anatomical structures involved in the lower limb's posterior compartment.

 

A. represents the biceps femoris, a muscle of the posterior thigh.

 

B. represents the sciatic nerve, which was compressed in this case, leading to the patient's symptoms.

 

C. represents the popliteal vein, which runs behind the knee, alongside the sciatic nerve and the popliteal artery in the popliteal fossa. However, it does not run in between the vein and nerve; it runs parallel to them.

 

D. represents the semitendinosus muscle, a muscle in the posterior thigh. Both A and D arise from the ischial tuberosity of the pelvis, explaining their common point of origin.

 

Educational objectives:

 

In cases of sciatica, the sciatic nerve is the primary structure affected, leading to radiating pain down the leg. The muscles of the posterior thigh, such as the biceps femoris and semitendinosus, originate from the ischial tuberosity, while the popliteal vein runs alongside the nerve and artery behind the knee.

questions.stemHtml: A patient died due to a malignant neck tumor. A neck dissection was done to understand the extent of cancer for research purposes. All of the following statements are true except?

options.label: A
options.text: A emerges from the nerve point behind the sternocleidomastoid, runs superiorly, and divides into anterior & posterior divisions.

options.label: B
options.text: B is the 1st branch of the external carotid artery.

options.label: C
options.text: C is palpable along the lower margin of the mandible in front of the strongest muscle of the body.

options.label: D
options.text: D is showing its activity under the control of the facial nerve.

questions.answerText: B is the 1st branch of the external carotid artery.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) B is the 1st branch of the external carotid artery.

 

This question revolves around the anatomical structures of the neck and their relations, as depicted in the image, which shows a dissection of the neck region.

 

A. is identified as the great auricular nerve (GAN), which emerges from the nerve point behind the sternocleidomastoid and divides into anterior and posterior branches. It is responsible for sensory innervation of the skin around the ear and neck.

 

B. is the superior thyroid artery, which is one of the branches of the external carotid artery. However, it is not the first branch. The first branch of the external carotid artery is typically the ascending pharyngeal artery. This makes this option incorrect.

 

C. is the facial artery, which is palpable along the lower margin of the mandible. It supplies blood to the face, running near the strongest muscle in the body, the masseter muscle.

 

D. represents the submandibular gland, which is under the control of the facial nerve through parasympathetic fibers. The facial nerve stimulates the secretion of saliva through its connection with the submandibular ganglion.

 

Educational objectives:

 

The superior thyroid artery is not the first branch of the external carotid artery; instead, the ascending pharyngeal artery holds that distinction. Understanding the relationships of these key neck structures is essential in surgical procedures such as neck dissections.

questions.stemHtml: A 21-year-old nulligravida Caucasian patient presented with a 15-month history of amenorrhea, bifrontal headache, and photophobia. Examination revealed general physical, neurologic, and ophthalmoscopic findings with normal visual fields. A pelvic examination revealed normal external genitalia, a nulliparous cervix and uterus, and bilateral cystic ovarian masses measuring 8 cm in diameter on the right and 4 cm on the left. Endocrine evaluation revealed an elevated serum prolactin in the range of 48 to 50 ng/ml. This situation was related to a mass in which of the following areas in the image below?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) B

 

The patient presented with a combination of amenorrhea, bifrontal headache, photophobia, and elevated prolactin levels ranging from 48 to 50 ng/ml, which is consistent with a diagnosis of hyperprolactinemia. The cause of this hyperprolactinemia is likely a prolactinoma, which is a pituitary tumor leading to an overproduction of prolactin.

 

B refers to the sella turcica, a saddle-shaped depression in the sphenoid bone that houses the pituitary gland. This location is crucial because the pituitary gland regulates the secretion of multiple hormones, including prolactin. A tumor in this region (a prolactinoma) can cause an increase in prolactin levels, leading to the patient’s symptoms such as amenorrhea and galactorrhea.

 

The elevated prolactin results in:

 

Galactorrhea, which is the abnormal production of breast milk.

 

Amenorrhea, or the absence of menstrual periods, due to prolactin's inhibitory effect on the secretion of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH).

 

In this case, the mass in the sella turcica caused the pituitary gland to overproduce prolactin, leading to the patient's hormonal imbalance. The patient’s symptoms and the presence of elevated prolactin confirm that the issue is related to a pituitary mass in the sella turcica.

 

Other options:

 

Option A. Cribriform plate: This is the cribriform plate, which is part of the ethmoid bone and allows for the passage of the olfactory nerves (cranial nerve I). A lesion here would typically cause issues related to the sense of smell (anosmia) rather than the hormonal disturbances seen in this patient.

Ans. D) In childhood, individual sacral vertebrae are connected by intervertebral discs, and the adult bone retains many vertebral features.

 

The bone shown in the image is the sacrum, a large triangular bone that is formed by the fusion of five sacral vertebrae. It is an integral structure in the pelvis, forming the back portion and helping to connect the spine to the pelvic girdle.

 

Option D. This is false. During childhood, the sacral vertebrae are separated by intervertebral discs, but as the individual matures, these vertebrae fuse to form a single bone. In adulthood, the sacrum does not retain the intervertebral discs that were present during childhood, although it does retain certain vertebral features like the spinal canal and remnants of vertebral bodies.

 

Other Options

 

Option A. This is true. The sacrum is indeed a fusion of five vertebrae and forms the posterosuperior wall of the pelvic cavity. It is wedged between the two innominate (hip) bones.

 

Option B. This is true. The sacrum's blunted caudal apex articulates with the coccyx, while its superior base articulates with the fifth lumbar vertebra at the lumbosacral angle.

 

Option C. This is true. The sacrum is set obliquely and curved. The dorsal surface is convex while the ventral surface is concave, which increases pelvic capacity and allows for better pelvic organ accommodation.

 

Educational objectives:

 

In adulthood, the sacrum is a solid, fused bone with no intervertebral discs, unlike in childhood when the vertebrae are separated by discs. Understanding the fusion of the sacral vertebrae and the anatomical features of the sacrum is important in studying the structure of the pelvis.

Option C. B: refers to the right gastric artery, which supplies the lower portion of the stomach, but it is not directly involved in bleeding from Type IV ulcers.

 

Educational objectives:

questions.stem: Which is not a cause of positive Trendelenburg sign?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Paralysis of gluteus maximus

 

 

The Trendelenburg sign is positive when there is weakness in the gluteus medius and gluteus minimus, muscles that stabilize the pelvis during the stance phase of walking. A positive sign indicates that the pelvis drops on the side opposite to the affected muscles. This occurs due to paralysis or weakness of the gluteus medius and minimus or damage to the superior gluteal nerve, which innervates them.

 

The gluteus maximus, however, plays a different role in hip extension rather than pelvic stabilization during walking, so its paralysis is not a cause of a positive Trendelenburg sign.

 

Other options:
 

Option B. Paralysis of gluteus medius & minimus: These muscles are the primary stabilizers of the pelvis during walking. Paralysis of these muscles leads to a positive Trendelenburg sign.
 

Option C. Damage to superior gluteal nerve: The superior gluteal nerve innervates the gluteus medius and minimus, so any damage to this nerve results in a positive Trendelenburg sign.
 

Option D. Damage to tensor fascia lata: The tensor fascia lata, also innervated by the superior gluteal nerve, assists the gluteus medius and minimus in stabilizing the pelvis. Damage to this muscle could contribute to a positive Trendelenburg sign.

 

Educational objectives:
 

A positive Trendelenburg sign is caused by weakness or paralysis of the gluteus medius and minimus muscles or damage to the superior gluteal nerve, not the gluteus maximus.

The popliteus muscle is a small muscle located in the posterior compartment of the leg, specifically in the popliteal fossa. Its primary function is to unlock the knee joint by rotating the femur on the tibia during the initiation of flexion. The tibial nerve, a branch of the sciatic nerve, provides the nerve supply to the popliteus muscle, ensuring its proper function.

 

Other options:

Option C. Common peroneal nerve: The common peroneal nerve is a branch of the sciatic nerve but supplies muscles in the anterior and lateral 

compartments of the leg, not the popliteus.
Option D. Deep peroneal nerve: The deep peroneal nerve is a branch of the common peroneal nerve and primarily supplies muscles involved in dorsiflexion and toe extension, not the popliteus muscle.

 

Educational objectives:
 

The popliteus muscle is supplied by the tibial nerve, which is responsible for its function in knee joint movements.

The vastus medialis, part of the quadriceps femoris muscle group, plays a crucial role in the locking mechanism of the knee. It helps in the final stages of knee extension and stabilizes the patella. Specifically, the vastus medialis oblique (VMO) fibers are responsible for ensuring that the knee "locks" during full extension, which provides stability during standing. the vastus medialis is emphasized as the key muscle involved in this mechanism.

 

Other options:

Option B. Rectus femoris: While rectus femoris is part of the quadriceps group and assists in knee extension, it is not directly responsible for knee locking.

questions.stem: Which muscle originates from the anterior superior iliac spine?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Sartorius

 

 

The sartorius muscle originates from the anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS). It is the longest muscle in the body, running obliquely across the thigh and inserting on the medial surface of the tibia. The sartorius plays an important role in hip flexion, abduction, and lateral rotation of the thigh, as well as knee flexion.

 

Other options:
 

Option A. Iliofemoral ligament: This is a ligament, not a muscle, that originates from the ilium and attaches to the femur. It is part of the hip joint capsule.
 

Option C. Vastus lateralis: This muscle originates from the greater trochanter and the linea aspera of the femur, not the ASIS.
 

Option D. Vastus medialis: This muscle also originates from the femur (the intertrochanteric line and medial lip of the linea aspera), not from the ASIS.

 

Educational objectives:
 

The sartorius muscle originates from the anterior superior iliac spine and is involved in movements of both the hip and knee joints.

questions.stem: Which bone in the foot is not attached by any muscle?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Talus

 

 

The talus is unique because it is the only bone in the foot that does not have any muscle or tendon attachments. It primarily functions as a connector between the leg and the foot, forming the lower part of the ankle joint and transferring weight across the foot. The talus articulates with other bones (tibia, fibula, calcaneum, and navicular) to enable movements but does not serve as an attachment site for muscles.

 

Other options:
 

Option B. Calcaneum: The calcaneum, or heel bone, is attached to several muscles, including the gastrocnemius and soleus muscles via the Achilles tendon.
 

Option C. Metatarsals: The metatarsals are connected to numerous muscles in the foot responsible for toe movements and foot stability.
 

Option D. Fibula: The fibula is a bone in the leg (not technically in the foot) and has attachments for muscles such as the peroneus longus and peroneus brevis.

 

Educational objectives:


The talus is the only bone in the foot without any muscle or tendon attachments.

questions.stem: Which muscle originates from the ischial tuberosity?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D. All of the above (Semimembranosus, Semitendinosus, Adductor magnus)


The ischial tuberosity serves as the origin point for multiple muscles of the posterior thigh. The semimembranosus, semitendinosus, adductor magnus (ischial head), and biceps femoris (long head) all originate from this bony prominence. These muscles are collectively known as the hamstring muscles and are essential for actions like hip extension and knee flexion. all these muscles share the same origin on the ischial tuberosity.

 

Educational objectives:


The ischial tuberosity is the common origin point for several important posterior thigh muscles, including the semimembranosus, semitendinosus, adductor magnus (ischial head), and biceps femoris (long head).

questions.stem: Femoral triangle base is formed by:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Inguinal ligament


The base of the femoral triangle is formed by the inguinal ligament. This structure runs between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic tubercle, providing support to the superior boundary of the femoral triangle. The femoral triangle's other borders are formed by the medial border of the sartorius muscle and the medial border of the adductor longus muscle, with the floor composed of muscles like the iliacus, psoas major, and pectineus.

 

Other options:
 

Option A. Medial border of sartorius: This forms the lateral boundary, not the base of the femoral triangle.
 

Option C. Medial border of adductor longus: This forms the medial boundary, not the base.
 

Option D. Iliacus: This muscle forms part of the floor of the femoral triangle, not the base.

 

Educational objectives:


The base of the femoral triangle is formed by the inguinal ligament.

questions.stem: Tibial and common peroneal nerve supplies:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Biceps femoris muscle


The biceps femoris muscle, particularly the long head, is a hybrid muscle that is supplied by both the tibial nerve (for the long head) and the common peroneal nerve (for the short head), which are branches of the sciatic nerve. This dual innervation allows for both hip extension and knee flexion. the biceps femoris is explicitly mentioned as being innervated by both the tibial and common peroneal nerves.

 

Other options:
 

Option A. Adductor magnus muscle: While the ischial head of the adductor magnus is also a hybrid muscle, it is innervated by the obturator and sciatic nerves, not the common peroneal nerve.
 

Option B. Adductor longus muscle: This muscle is innervated by the obturator nerve, not the tibial or common peroneal nerve.
 

Option C. Gracilis muscle: The gracilis is innervated by the obturator nerve and does not receive innervation from the tibial or common peroneal nerve.

 

Educational objectives:


The biceps femoris is a hybrid muscle, with the long head supplied by the tibial nerve and the short head by the common peroneal nerve.

questions.stem: Which of the following muscles is an evertor of the foot?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Peroneus longus muscle


Both the peroneus longus >peroneus brevis muscles are responsible for eversion of the foot. These muscles, located in the lateral compartment of the leg, work by pulling the foot outward, away from the midline. The peroneus longus also plays a role in plantarflexion. The combination of these two muscles ensures lateral stability of the ankle.

 

Other options:
 

Option A. Tibialis anterior muscle: This muscle is primarily responsible for dorsiflexion and inversion of the foot, not eversion.
 

Option B. Tibialis posterior: This muscle contributes to plantarflexion and inversion of the foot.

 

Educational objectives:


The muscles involved in eversion of the foot are the peroneus longus and peroneus brevis.

questions.stem: What is true about the iliotibial tract?

options.label: B
options.text: Gluteus medius is inserted into it

options.label: C
options.text: Insertion at medial aspect of tibia

options.label: D
options.text: Runs along the medial aspect of thigh

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Thickening of fascia lata


The iliotibial tract is a thickening of the fascia lata that extends from the ilium to the lateral side of the tibia. It provides lateral stability to the knee and assists in movements like flexion and abduction of the hip. Contrary to other options, the gluteus maximus inserts into the iliotibial tract, not the gluteus medius. The tract inserts on the lateral aspect of the tibia, not the medial, and it runs along the lateral aspect of the thigh.

 

Other options:
 

Option B. Gluteus medius is inserted into it: Incorrect, as the gluteus maximus inserts into the iliotibial tract, not the gluteus medius.
 

Option C. Insertion at medial aspect of tibia: Incorrect, the iliotibial tract inserts at the lateral aspect of the tibia.
 

Option D. Runs along the medial aspect of thigh: Incorrect, the iliotibial tract runs along the lateral aspect of the thigh.

 

Educational objectives:


The iliotibial tract is a thickening of the fascia lata that provides lateral stability to the knee by running along the lateral aspect of the thigh.

questions.stem: Which muscle is responsible for sitting to standing position?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Gluteus maximus


The gluteus maximus is the primary muscle responsible for hip extension, which is the key movement in transitioning from a sitting to a standing position. It is the largest and strongest extensor of the hip joint and plays a crucial role in stabilizing the body during this movement.

 

Other options:
 

Option A. Gluteus medius: This muscle primarily assists with hip abduction and stabilization but does not play a major role in standing from a sitting position.
 

Option C. Gluteus minimus: Similar to the gluteus medius, it is involved in abduction and stabilization of the hip.
 

Option D. Tensor fascia lata: This muscle assists in hip flexion and stabilization but is not responsible for the sitting-to-standing movement.

 

Educational objectives:


The gluteus maximus is the chief extensor muscle that powers the movement from sitting to standing.

questions.stem: Gluteus medius is supplied by:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Superior gluteal nerve


The gluteus medius is supplied by the superior gluteal nerve, which originates from the L4, L5, and S1 nerve roots. This nerve passes above the piriformis muscle and innervates the gluteus medius, allowing it to play a crucial role in hip abduction and stabilizing the pelvis during walking.

 

Other options:


Option B. Inferior gluteal nerve: This nerve supplies the gluteus maximus, not the gluteus medius.


Option C. Nerve to obturator internus: This nerve supplies the obturator internus muscle, not the gluteus medius.


Option D. Nerve to quadratus femoris: This nerve supplies the quadratus femoris muscle, not the gluteus medius.

 

Educational objectives:


The gluteus medius is innervated by the superior gluteal nerve, which is important for hip abduction and pelvic stability during walking.

questions.stem: In injury to the neck of fibula, which of the following nerve is usually injured?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Common peroneal nerve


The common peroneal nerve winds around the neck of the fibula, making it susceptible to injury in this region. Any trauma or injury to the neck of the fibula can compress or damage the common peroneal nerve, leading to conditions such as foot drop or weakness in foot dorsiflexion and eversion.

 

Other options:
 

Option A. Superficial peroneal nerve: This nerve branches from the common peroneal nerve and supplies muscles in the lateral compartment of the leg. However, it is not directly involved in injuries at the neck of the fibula.
 

Option B. Deep peroneal nerve: This is a branch of the common peroneal nerve but is not directly at risk at the neck of the fibula.
 

Option D. Tibial nerve: The tibial nerve runs in the posterior compartment of the leg and is not affected by injuries to the neck of the fibula.

 

Educational objectives:


Injuries to the neck of the fibula commonly affect the common peroneal nerve, which can result in foot drop.

questions.stem: During the South Africa test match, Indian captain Rohit Sharma got stretching of muscles at the thigh during running in between the wickets. Which muscles are stretched, known as Runner’s muscles?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Hamstring muscles


The hamstring muscles are commonly referred to as the Runner’s muscles. These muscles, which include the biceps femoris, semitendinosus, and semimembranosus, are located at the back of the thigh and are often stretched during high-speed activities such as running, particularly during quick acceleration or deceleration. In activities like cricket, sudden bursts of speed while running between wickets can cause the hamstrings to stretch or strain, which is a common injury among athletes.

 

Other options:
 

Option A. Quadriceps femoris: This muscle group is responsible for knee extension and is less likely to be injured during running compared to the hamstrings.
 

Option B. Adductor muscles: These muscles are involved in thigh adduction and stabilization but are not the primary muscles involved in running.
 

Option C. Gluteal muscles: These muscles help with hip extension and abduction but are not typically referred to as Runner’s muscles.

 

Educational objectives:


The hamstring muscles are responsible for hip extension and knee flexion, making them prone to stretching or injury during running activities, earning them the name Runner's muscles.

questions.stem: What is the nerve root value of the superior gluteal nerve?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) L4, L5, S1

 

 

The superior gluteal nerve has a root value of L4, L5, S1. It supplies muscles such as the gluteus medius, gluteus minimus, and tensor fascia lata, playing a crucial role in hip abduction and stabilization during gait. The superior gluteal nerve exits through the greater sciatic foramen above the piriformis muscle.

 

Educational objectives:
 

The superior gluteal nerve originates from the L4, L5, and S1 nerve roots, supplying key muscles responsible for hip abduction.

questions.stem: What is the root value of the sciatic nerve?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) L4, L5, S1, S2, S3

 

 

The sciatic nerve is the largest nerve in the body, and its root value is L4, L5, S1, S2, S3. It supplies the muscles of the posterior thigh and all muscles below the knee. The sciatic nerve divides into the tibial and common peroneal nerves, and its wide distribution makes it critical for lower limb movement and sensation.

 

Educational objectives:


The root value of the sciatic nerve is L4, L5, S1, S2, S3.

questions.stem: Tibialis posterior muscle is supplied by which nerve?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Tibial nerve


The tibialis posterior muscle, located in the posterior compartment of the leg, is supplied by the tibial nerve. This nerve, a branch of the sciatic nerve, innervates the muscles of the posterior leg, including the tibialis posterior. The tibial nerve plays a key role in controlling plantarflexion and inversion of the foot.

 

Other options:


Option B. Deep peroneal nerve: This nerve supplies muscles in the anterior compartment of the leg, such as the tibialis anterior, but not the tibialis posterior.


Option C. Femoral nerve: This nerve innervates the muscles in the anterior thigh, including the quadriceps, but does not supply the tibialis posterior.


Option D. Sural nerve: The sural nerve provides sensory innervation to the posterior and lateral aspect of the leg and foot but does not supply the tibialis posterior.

 

Educational objectives:


The tibialis posterior muscle is supplied by the tibial nerve, which controls plantarflexion and inversion of the foot.

questions.stemHtml: Mention the type of joint present at the marked region.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Saddle

 

The marked region is at the first carpometacarpal joint (thumb), which is a saddle joint. This type of joint allows movements in two planes: flexion-extension and abduction-adduction, as well as a combination of movements for thumb opposition. The saddle joint between the trapezium and the base of the first metacarpal allows the thumb to have a wide range of motion, including the ability to touch the fingertips, which is vital for grip and dexterity.

 

Other options:
 

Option A. Ellipsoid: This joint allows movement in two planes but lacks the range of opposition provided by the saddle joint.
 

Option B. Condylar: Condylar joints allow for movement but do not provide the same degree of freedom as a saddle joint.
 

Option C. Plane: Plane joints only allow gliding movements, found between carpal bones, not at the thumb.

 

Educational objectives:

questions.stemHtml: Identify the muscle forming the marked boundary.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Extensor Pollicis Longus

 

 

The image points to the anatomical snuffbox, a triangular depression on the lateral aspect of the wrist. The boundaries of this snuffbox are formed by the tendons of the extensor pollicis longus (posteriorly), and the abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis (anteriorly). The marked muscle in this image corresponds to the extensor pollicis longus, which forms the posterior boundary of the anatomical snuffbox.

 

Other options:
 

Option A. Extensor Pollicis Brevis: This muscle forms the anterior boundary of the snuffbox but is not the marked muscle in this image.
 

Option B. Abductor Pollicis Longus: This muscle also forms part of the anterior boundary of the snuffbox but is not the correct answer.
 

Option C. Abductor Pollicis Brevis: This muscle is not part of the anatomical snuffbox and does not form any boundary.

 

Educational objectives:
 

The extensor pollicis longus forms the posterior boundary of the anatomical snuffbox and is the correct identification for the marked muscle in the image.

questions.stemHtml: In the given image, the tendon marked by the arrow is?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Flexor carpi radialis

 

 

The flexor carpi radialis (FCR) tendon is located on the radial side of the forearm. It is responsible for flexing and abducting the wrist. In the image, the arrow marks the position of the FCR tendon, which lies lateral to the palmaris longus tendon (if present) and is easily palpable during wrist flexion.

 

Other options:
 

Option B. Flexor carpi ulnaris: This tendon is located on the ulnar (pinky) side of the forearm and does not correspond to the marked position in the image.
 

Option C. Flexor digitorum superficialis: This tendon lies deeper and is not as easily palpable as the FCR.
 

Option D. Palmaris longus: This tendon, if present, would be positioned more medially compared to the flexor carpi radialis.

 

Educational objectives:


The flexor carpi radialis is a prominent tendon located on the radial side of the wrist and is marked in the image.

questions.stemHtml: Which muscle is attached to the marked bony structure?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Iliopsoas

 

The bony structure marked by the arrow is the lesser trochanter of the femur. The iliopsoas muscle, which is a combination of the iliacus and psoas major muscles, inserts on the lesser trochanter. This muscle plays a crucial role in hip flexion and is the strongest flexor of the thigh at the hip joint.

 

Other options:
 

Option B. Gluteus maximus: This muscle inserts on the gluteal tuberosity of the femur and the iliotibial tract, not the lesser trochanter.
 

Option C. Gluteus medius: This muscle inserts on the greater trochanter of the femur, not the lesser trochanter.
 

Option D. Sartorius: The sartorius inserts on the pes anserinus, which is on the medial surface of the tibia, not the femur.

 

Educational objectives:


The iliopsoas muscle inserts on the lesser trochanter of the femur, making it the primary muscle responsible for hip flexion.

questions.stem: Common carotid artery pulse is taken at the level of:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Cricoid cartilage

 

The common carotid artery pulse is typically taken at the level of the cricoid cartilage, which is located around the C6 vertebra. This is a critical anatomical landmark where the common carotid artery can be easily palpated by compressing it against the transverse processes of the cervical vertebrae.

 

Other options:
 

Option B. Laryngeal prominence: This is the location of the Adam's apple, which is higher up in the neck and not the typical place for palpating the carotid pulse.
 

Option C. Suprasternal notch: This is located at the top of the sternum, lower than the level of the cricoid cartilage and not ideal for palpating the carotid artery.
 

Option D. Angle of mandible: This is a landmark for the facial artery and is not the typical site for assessing the common carotid pulse.

 

Educational objectives:


The common carotid artery pulse is most commonly palpated at the level of the cricoid cartilage.

questions.stem: What is the arrangement from near to far of the recti muscles attached towards the limbus?

options.label: A
options.text: Medial rectus, inferior rectus, lateral rectus, superior rectus

options.label: B
options.text: Superior rectus, lateral rectus, inferior rectus, medial rectus

options.label: C
options.text: Medial rectus, lateral rectus, inferior rectus, superior rectus

options.label: D
options.text: Medial rectus, superior rectus, lateral rectus, inferior rectus

questions.answerText: Medial rectus, inferior rectus, lateral rectus, superior rectus
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Medial rectus, inferior rectus, lateral rectus, superior rectus


The recti muscles of the eye attach around the limbus, with the nearest muscle being the medial rectus, followed by the inferior rectus, then the lateral rectus, and finally the superior rectus. This arrangement is based on their proximity to the limbus (the sclerocorneal junction).

 

 

Educational objectives:


The order of the recti muscles attaching to the eye from nearest to farthest from the limbus is: medial rectus, inferior rectus, lateral rectus, and superior rectus.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old patient was brought to the ER following a suspected stroke. The patient was unable to speak fluently, though he understands the given instructions. Which category of aphasia is most likely present in the patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Broca’s aphasia

 

Broca’s aphasia, also known as non-fluent aphasia, is characterized by the patient's inability to speak fluently, but they still understand spoken and written language. This condition occurs due to damage to Broca's area, located in the inferior frontal gyrus of the brain, often as a result of a stroke. Patients with Broca’s aphasia have difficulty forming complete sentences and may speak in short, broken phrases.

 

 

Other options:
 

Option B. Wernicke’s aphasia: In Wernicke’s aphasia, patients speak fluently but their speech is often nonsensical or irrelevant, and they have poor comprehension, which is not the case here.
 

Option C. Conduction aphasia: This type of aphasia involves an inability to repeat words or phrases, but speech remains fluent and comprehension is generally intact.
 

Option D. Global aphasia: This is the most severe form of aphasia, involving both speech production and comprehension difficulties, which does not match this patient’s presentation.

 

Educational objectives:
 

Broca’s aphasia presents as an inability to speak fluently, while comprehension remains intact, typically caused by damage to the inferior frontal gyrus.

questions.stem: While administering epidural anesthesia, which structure is not punctured before injecting the drug?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Arachnoid mater


During epidural anesthesia, the needle is introduced through the skin and several layers, including the supraspinous ligament, interspinous ligament, and ligamentum flavum, before reaching the epidural space. The arachnoid mater, however, is not pierced in this procedure, as it lies deeper, covering the spinal cord and cerebrospinal fluid. Piercing the arachnoid mater would lead to a subarachnoid (spinal) injection, which is different from an epidural.

 

Educational objectives:


In epidural anesthesia, the arachnoid mater is not punctured; the drug is delivered just outside this layer, in the epidural space.

questions.stemHtml: Identify the marked chamber.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Left atrium


In the given image, the marked chamber corresponds to the left atrium. The left atrium is located posteriorly in the heart and is part of the systemic circulation where oxygenated blood from the lungs enters before being pumped into the left ventricle. The anatomy of the left atrium is such that it forms part of the posterior surface of the heart, which is visible in radiographic views.

 

Other options:
 

Option A. Right atrium: The right atrium is positioned on the right border of the heart and is responsible for receiving deoxygenated blood from the systemic circulation, not the marked structure in the image.
 

Option C. Right ventricle: The right ventricle forms the anterior surface of the heart and is not the chamber marked in this image.
 

Option D. Left ventricle: While the left ventricle is located near the left atrium, it is typically more inferior and anterior, and does not correspond to the marked structure.

 

Educational objectives:


The left atrium, located posteriorly in the heart, is the chamber marked in this image and plays a key role in receiving oxygenated blood from the lungs.

questions.stemHtml: The marked line corresponds to which vertebral level?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) L3

 

The marked line corresponds to the L3 vertebral level. Clinically, the line drawn between the highest points of the iliac crests is often used as a reference point to identify the L3-L4 vertebral interspace. This level is crucial, particularly for procedures such as lumbar punctures, as it provides a safe entry point to avoid damage to the spinal cord, which usually ends at the L1-L2 level in adults.

 

Other options:

 

Option A. T12: T12 is located at the thoracolumbar junction, much higher than the line shown in the image.


Option B. L1: While L1 is closer, the line of the iliac crests is generally below this vertebra.


Option C. L2: L2 is near, but the iliac crest line more commonly intersects at the L3 level, which is more commonly used as a landmark.

 

Educational objectives:

 

The iliac crest line is a reliable landmark for identifying the L3 vertebral level, important in procedures like lumbar puncture.

questions.stem: Which structure forms the lateral boundary of Hesselbach’s triangle?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Inferior epigastric vessels

 

Hesselbach's triangle is an important anatomical region, especially in the context of inguinal hernias. The lateral boundary of Hesselbach’s triangle is formed by the inferior epigastric vessels. This triangle is significant because direct inguinal hernias often occur through it, making the recognition of its boundaries crucial in clinical anatomy.

 

Other options:

 

Option A. Femoral vessels: These vessels are located below the inguinal ligament and are not involved in the boundaries of Hesselbach's triangle.
 

Option C. Inguinal ligament: The inguinal ligament forms the inferior boundary of Hesselbach's triangle, not the lateral boundary.
 

Option D. Rectus abdominis: The rectus abdominis forms the medial boundary of Hesselbach's triangle.

 

Educational objectives:

 

The inferior epigastric vessels form the lateral boundary of Hesselbach's triangle, a critical site for direct inguinal hernias.

questions.stemHtml: Identify the structures marked in numbers.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) 1- liver, 2- pancreas, 3- spleen

 

The structures marked in the image are identified as follows:
 

1.  Liver: which is located on the right side of the abdomen and plays a key role in digestion and metabolism.
 

2.  Pancreas: which lies behind the stomach and produces important enzymes and hormones such as insulin.
 

3.  Spleen: located on the left side of the abdomen, helps filter blood as part of the immune system.

 

Educational objectives:

 

The image correctly identifies the liver, pancreas, and spleen as structures 1, 2, and 3, respectively.

questions.stem: For the conjoint tendon, all are true except?

options.label: A
options.text: Formed by the internal oblique aponeurosis and transversus abdominis aponeurosis

options.label: B
options.text: Forms the posterior wall of the inguinal canal

options.label: C
options.text: Protects the superficial inguinal ring to maintain the integrity of the inguinal canal

options.label: D
options.text: Runs parallel to the inguinal ligament

questions.answerText: Runs parallel to the inguinal ligament
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Runs parallel to the inguinal ligament

 

The conjoint tendon is formed by the aponeuroses of the internal oblique and transversus abdominis muscles. It plays a key role in forming the posterior wall of the inguinal canal and provides protection to the superficial inguinal ring to help maintain the canal's structural integrity. The incorrect statement is that the conjoint tendon "runs parallel to the inguinal ligament," which it does not.

 

Other options:

 

Option A. Formed by the internal oblique aponeurosis and transversus abdominis aponeurosis: This is correct; the conjoint tendon is made from these two aponeuroses.
 

Option B. Forms the posterior wall of the inguinal canal: This is accurate; the conjoint tendon forms a crucial part of the posterior wall.
 

Option C. Protects the superficial inguinal ring to maintain the integrity of the inguinal canal: Correct; this is another vital function of the conjoint tendon.

 

Educational objectives:

 

The conjoint tendon forms the posterior wall of the inguinal canal and is made up of the aponeuroses of the internal oblique and transversus abdominis muscles, but it does not run parallel to the inguinal ligament.
